paragraphs: Loudoun County supervisors voted 7-1-1 on September 15 to prepare a pause of up to 12 months on final board votes for data center and substation applications that need legislative approval. The resolution has not yet been adopted: the county plans to consider it October 20. Under the proposal, administrative applications and Planning Commission work could continue, and some projects may qualify for exceptions.

The county changed its zoning rules in March 2025 so most new data centers need a public hearing, with an exception for qualifying applications already under review. Data centers now supply 38% of Loudoun's general fund revenue, which has helped pay for schools, a $102 million recreation center and a public park. Supervisor Juli Briskman said the growth had gone too far; Kristen Umstattd opposed drafting the pause and Caleb Kershner abstained.

In Sterling, residents near Vantage Data Centers' Ashburn II campus on Glenn Drive have complained about noise and diesel fumes. After a July 16 power failure, the campus ran backup generators into the following evening. One homeowner told WJLA the generator exhaust irritated her throat and lungs and sometimes woke her at night. Supervisors are scheduled to consider changes to the earlier-application exception October 6, before considering the proposed pause October 20.

Project Baccara, a data center campus with its own 700-megawatt gas power plant, is planned on 160 acres about a mile north of Luke Air Force Base in Maricopa County, near Glendale and Surprise. On May 6 the Board of Supervisors voted 4-1 to give it the military compatibility permit it needed, with Steve Gallardo voting no. The developer is Takanock, a Michigan-based data center firm. The site is unincorporated county land, and Glendale has voted to begin annexing it.

The plan would put two data centers and the gas plant about 400 feet from about a dozen homes. The county received 553 emails against it, more than 8,000 petition signatures and five emails in support. "Why would anybody think this would be a good site, so close to homes, so close to the end of a runway," said April Butler, whose family has lived in Surprise for six generations. The developer's lawyer told the board its chief executive had accepted all of the Air Force's conditions in writing.

Baccara is one of 71 data center campuses planned or running in the county, the Arizona Republic counted. The largest running today include Stream Data Centers' 157-acre campus in Goodyear, with 280 megawatts of capacity and two of seven buildings finished.

Most of Virginia's data centers are in Northern Virginia: Loudoun County alone has about 50 tracked sites, most of them in Ashburn, followed by Prince William and Fairfax counties. Loudoun supervisors voted 7-1-1 on September 15 to draft a pause of up to 12 months on board votes for new data center and substation applications, and the board is scheduled to vote on it October 20. Farther south, big campuses are under construction in Stafford, Spotsylvania, Louisa and Caroline counties.

Residents have stopped several large projects this year. In Prince William County, developers gave up the court fight over the 1,760-acre Digital Gateway in July, and less than a week later supervisors rejected Dulles Cloud South, which would have been the largest data center project in county history. Hanover County supervisors voted 4-3 in May to deny Tract's 430-acre Mountain Road Technology Park after months of review. In Franklin County, a proposed Crusoe data center at Summit View Business Park near Rocky Mount was dropped in August after residents organized.

On September 18 Gov. Abigail Spanberger signed Executive Order 22, which requires local approval for projects using more than 25 megawatts of power, sets stricter standards for energy, water and noise, and bans secrecy agreements between data centers and state agencies. It is not a moratorium, which some opponents are still calling for. Loudoun's board also takes up changes to its rules for projects already in the pipeline on October 6.

Georgia's biggest data center plan is Project Camellia, a campus of about 1,400 acres near Rincon in Effingham County that Octans Georgia, an OpenAI affiliate, plans to build. It could need up to 3.2 gigawatts (3,200 megawatts) of power. The county commission was due to vote on the plan September 15, then gave itself more time; no new date has been announced, and two lawsuits over the approvals are pending in Effingham County Superior Court.

In September, five residents and the environmental group One Hundred Miles sued the county's Industrial Development Authority, saying its July vote to commit the land to Octans and give it a 50% property tax break went ahead without proper notice or a meaningful agenda. Three other residents sued September 2 over the August zoning change that allows data centers on industrial land, saying the required hearings were skipped. "We bought into that neighborhood, into that area, because we wanted the quiet right to enjoyment," plaintiff Raymond Carver, who lives near the site, told the Effingham Herald.

Power is the statewide question. In December 2025 state regulators voted 5-0 to let Georgia Power add about 10,000 megawatts, 80% of it for data centers, at a construction cost of $16.3 billion; commission staff said customers would pay $50 billion to $60 billion over the coming decades. Georgia Power's chief executive, Chris Womack, told shareholders that once the OpenAI contract is confirmed, the utility will have promised about one gigawatt more than it has permission to provide.

Most other projects are around Atlanta and in the counties west and south of it. In Augusta, residents of the Haynes Station subdivision are fighting QTS's data center on Gordon Highway, an expanded version of a project approved before their homes were built; the commission's 49-day pause in June did not cover it. Local governments from Cobb and DeKalb counties to Valdosta and Albany now have 31 pauses on new data centers in force.

Chicago's mayor wants to stop new data centers in the city, and the fight over whether he can is now the county's main data center story. On August 11, 2026, Mayor Brandon Johnson called for a temporary moratorium on new or expanded data centers until permanent rules are written, and signed an executive order requiring closer review of diesel generator air permits, noise limits on generators and cooling equipment, and an assessment of power demand, water use and neighborhood effects for planned developments. "Chicagoans have been absolutely clear," he said. A moratorium needs a City Council vote, and Zoning Committee Chair Gilbert Villegas (36th) called the order "another political stunt by the mayor." Chicago has 39 data centers, most in or near downtown, and Cook County has 109 with 12 more planned, part of what CBRE ranks as the country's fourth-largest data center market.

The sharpest local anger is on the Southeast Side. Related Digital announced in March 2025 that it would build a hyperscale data center of about 1 gigawatt at the north end of Quantum Shore, the $9 billion quantum computing development on the former U.S. Steel South Works site, which is getting $500 million in state money and an estimated $175 million in county tax breaks over 30 years. At a Southside Together town hall at Arnold Mireles Academy in August, the crowd chanted "Shut it down" and booed Johnson when he declined to halt the project. "This facility threatens our peace," said South Chicago resident Reneé Redmond, 67. Johnson said no data center is planned as part of the campus, and the city's business affairs department said it had no pending license application for the data center site. Lia Terrell of Southside Together, who has lived in the area for 15 years, said the group would keep organizing "with or without the mayor."

The county's biggest concentration of data centers is not downtown but in the suburb of Elk Grove Village, near O'Hare, where ten projects on this record share an industrial corridor, including campuses run by Aligned, Digital Realty, Microsoft, Prime, STACK, Stream and T5. Most have not said publicly what stage they are at or how much power they will use.

In the suburbs the fights are site by site. In Hoffman Estates, Karis Critical wanted to rezone 186 acres at 4800 West Higgins Road, and on June 30, 2026 the landowner withdrew the application after residents learned that village staff had discussed it with the developer for about 18 months before it was made public, and that Village Manager Eric Palm had signed a letter pledging staff support. In July, Cicero's trustees passed resolutions opposing two rumored data centers, including one at Hawthorne Race Course in neighboring Stickney, saying they want none built anywhere near the town of more than 80,000 people.

The costs are what residents keep raising. ComEd customers' monthly charges rose about 12 percent in June, after double-digit increases the summer before, and ComEd's chief executive said in June that proposed data centers in Northern Illinois had requested 33 gigawatts. "If we're just looking at the impacts that data centers have on our electricity costs, there's not much the city of Chicago can do," said Sarah Moskowitz, executive director of the Citizen's Utility Board, who wants the state to act. Springfield has not: the POWER Act, which would have made data centers report water use, sign community benefit agreements and pay for their own renewable power, died without a vote when the session ended on May 31, and Gov. JB Pritzker paused new state data center tax incentives from July 1. State Sen. Darby Hills of Barrington Hills has filed Senate Bill 1050, which would bar data centers within three miles of a residential community without its consent.

The City Council still has to decide whether to take up Johnson's moratorium. Southside Together held a rally at 91st Street and Commercial Avenue on September 12, and both the POWER Act and Hills's bill are expected back in the fall veto session; until then, nothing proposed in Cook County is subject to the water reporting, community agreements or energy requirements the POWER Act contained.

San José is courting large new data centers, and the biggest are planned for Alviso, a small, low-lying neighborhood in the north of the city. Microsoft is building a 99-megawatt campus at 1657 Alviso-Milpitas Road with 224 natural gas generators; Google proposes research buildings drawing about 250 megawatts; and Prologis is negotiating for 159 acres of buffer land by the wastewater plant for data centers and research space using 496 megawatts. City staff plan to bring new data center standards to the City Council in December.

Residents want a moratorium until those standards are in place. "We're putting an entire city's worth of data centers in this tiny neighborhood, and the public health implications are unstudied," said San José resident Ellina Yin. In south San José, Prologis also proposes a 99-megawatt data center with 44 diesel generators on Silver Creek Valley Road. Mayor Matt Mahan promises "some of the highest, strictest standards in every category of concern" but opposes a pause. San José has about 20 data centers running, six under construction and five seeking approval.

Santa Clara, next door, has about 60 data centers, more than any other West Coast city, drawn by cheap power from the city-owned Silicon Valley Power. The limit there is the grid: Digital Realty and STACK have each finished a 48-megawatt building that stands empty until a $450 million utility upgrade is done in 2028. Council member and mayoral candidate Kevin Park wants to stop: "Let's stop building data centers." Gilroy, in the south of the county, has tightened its approvals.

On July 2, 2026 two companies called GW Acquisition Co. filed a notice withdrawing their petition to the Virginia Supreme Court, and with it the Prince William Digital Gateway died after five years. At full build it would have been the largest data center campus in the world: more than 22 million square feet across roughly 2,000 acres along Pageland Lane, running up against the boundary of Manassas National Battlefield Park.

It was beaten in court on process rather than on planning. The Board of County Supervisors approved the rezoning in December 2023 after a public hearing that ran 27 hours. In January 2024 the American Battlefield Trust and a group of residents sued, arguing the county had rushed the zoning and cut short the public's chance to be heard. In August 2025 Prince William Circuit Court Judge Kimberly Irving voided the rezonings over improper public notice, and in March 2026 the Virginia Court of Appeals upheld her. By April the county itself and the co-developer, Compass Datacenters, had both dropped out of the appeal, leaving QTS alone in it until July.

The county spent public money on the losing side. Supervisors put more than $1.7 million of taxpayer funds into defending the rezoning alongside the developers, including a further $400,000 approved as the case went on. The campaign against it ran to two lawsuits and two electoral recalls.

The appetite changed with the verdict. Less than a week after QTS walked away, the same board rejected a rezoning for Dulles Cloud South, another data center proposal on a site of about 2,000 acres. A county that had been the second-largest data center market in Northern Virginia after Loudoun had turned down two of the biggest schemes ever put to it inside a fortnight.

What happens next is a state question as much as a local one. Virginia's 2026 legislation now requires customers drawing 25 megawatts or more to carry the cost of the generating capacity built for them, and Governor Spanberger's Executive Order 22, signed on September 18, 2026, requires local approval for projects above that threshold and bans the non-disclosure agreements that kept deals like this one out of public view while they were being negotiated.

Texas has halted state approvals for new data centers. On September 21 Gov. Greg Abbott ordered the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality to issue no permits for data center projects until state audits of their power and water use are done, widening the freeze on new grid connections he ordered August 3. "Simply put, Texans must come first," Abbott wrote. The biggest projects under construction include Fermi America's HyperGrid in Carson County, IREN's campus at Sweetwater and SB Energy's sites in Milam County.

The audits ask developers for their electricity and water use, tax breaks, ownership and plans to limit harm to neighbors. Only about 28% of data centers answered a state water-use survey, and on September 14 Abbott told the Texas Water Development Board to penalize those that do not report. Counties have little power of their own: Hood County dropped a moratorium after state Sen. Paul Bettencourt said it had no legal authority, and Hill County rescinded one after a developer sued for $100 million.

Cities are acting too. San Marcos became the first Texas city to ban data centers, voting 4-3 on June 16 to make them ineligible anywhere in the city; Bettencourt says he will challenge the ban. Fort Worth's council voted unanimously in August to start a 90-day moratorium, which under state law needs public hearings first. The first hearing is set for November 10, and the pause would begin February 16, 2027.

Amazon is the biggest builder in Pennsylvania, with a pledge to spend $20 billion. It bought an existing data center and about 1,200 acres beside Talen Energy's nuclear plant in Salem Township, Luzerne County, where it plans up to 15 buildings, and plans a second campus in Falls Township, north of Philadelphia. It has applied for a local permit for 36 data centers at Homer City in Indiana County, next to a 4.5-gigawatt gas plant on the site of the state's largest former coal plant.

Local fights have stopped several projects. A 1,300-acre site in Hazle Township that Amazon is involved in was denied by local officials last year, and the developer has appealed. In Columbia Borough, Lancaster County, the council unanimously turned down a $6.4 million offer from Saadia Holdings to build on the former McGinness Airport land after more than 500 residents came to the meeting, organizer Taylor Enterline said. Projects in Blakely have also been blocked or delayed after public opposition.

Townships across the state have given themselves about six months to write data center rules using a state-law tool called a curative amendment, which works as a pause: Center, Adams and Lancaster townships in Butler County, Brookville in Jefferson County and Granville in Mifflin County among them. Once a township starts the process, it does not have to consider landowners' requests to add data centers to its zoning. In Granville, plans for a data center were filed two days before the vote.

In Harrisburg, the House and Senate each passed a repeal of the state's sales tax break on data center equipment in June, but neither version reached Gov. Josh Shapiro before the budget. The break is projected to cost $188.4 million in 2026-27. The Senate returned September 28 with 11 session days scheduled for the rest of the year.

Most of Ohio's big data centers sit around New Albany, in Licking and Franklin counties, where Meta, Google, Amazon, Microsoft, QTS and Vantage have campuses running or under construction. Towns elsewhere are pushing back: at least 138 Ohio towns and townships had data center moratoriums in force on September 17 and 23 had effectively banned them, by an Ohio Capital Journal count. A Bowling Green State University poll found 78% of Ohioans support a pause until more is known.

In Licking County, Pataskala City Council voted unanimously on August 25 to deny Aligned Data Centers' 200-megawatt plan, after hours of testimony. "We don't need a four-story building," resident Brandyn Bernard told the council. In Cleveland, the city rejected Lakeland Equity Group's $1.6 billion, 150-megawatt campus in Slavic Village in May. Jackson Township in southwestern Franklin County, next to Grove City, passed a one-year moratorium covering all its unincorporated land. Urbana, Lordstown and Commercial Point are being sued by developers over the moratoriums they passed.

Who pays for the power has been settled mostly by state regulators. Since July 2025, new data centers served by AEP Ohio must pay for at least 85% of the power capacity they reserve, whether they use it or not, and a House bill would extend that rule statewide. Pataskala voters decide in the November 3 election whether to allow data centers that use more than 25 megawatts.

Illinois' largest approved data center is the Joliet Technology Center, a campus of about 795 acres on farmland near Rowell and Bernhard roads, planned by Hillwood and PowerHouse Data Centers. The Joliet City Council approved it 8-1 in March 2026 after a public meeting that ran more than six hours. Yorkville approved Project Cardinal, a 1,037-acre campus along the Eldamain corridor, the same month, and the developers of Project Cardinal and Project Steel committed $91 million to the city over four years.

Cook County has 26 of the tracked sites, most of them established data centers in Elk Grove Village, Northlake, Des Plaines and at 350 East Cermak Road in Chicago. Elsewhere, residents have stopped projects. Karis Critical withdrew its request to rezone 186 acres at Higgins Road and Route 59 in Hoffman Estates on June 30, after the plan commission voted 4-2 against it and residents learned village staff had discussed the project with Karis for about 18 months before it became public. Karis had a similar proposal rejected in Naperville in January.

Projects in Rochelle, Pekin and Barrington Hills were also voted down or pulled this year, and eight towns and counties, including Lake County, Champaign County, Bloomington, Normal, Bourbonnais and Carbondale, have pauses on new data centers in force. Statewide, Governor JB Pritzker stopped signing new data center tax break agreements on July 1, 2026, after lawmakers did not pass the POWER Act, a bill regulating data centers' power and water use; lawmakers said it could return in the fall veto session. Plainfield's moratorium is set to end October 18.

California has 16 data center projects proposed or under construction, the most of them in Santa Clara County, but the sharpest local fights are in the Imperial and Coachella valleys. On September 9 an Imperial County judge overturned the county's approval of developer Sebastian Rucci's nearly 1-million-square-foot data center complex next to the Victoria Ranch neighborhood near the city of Imperial, and ordered a full environmental review. Rucci said he would seek a new trial and, failing that, appeal.

Imperial County supervisors paused all data center projects on county land in June and later extended the pause through May 2027; the city of Imperial did the same. A county advisory committee is due to report on zoning rules in January. "We are disappointed but not deterred," Rucci told KPBS after the ruling.

In the Coachella Valley, Coachella became the first Riverside County city to ban data centers permanently, after residents fought Stronghold Power Systems' planned campus at Avenue 52 and Fillmore Street. Indio extended its moratorium through October 16 while it drafts a ban, Desert Hot Springs extended its pause to two years, and Palm Springs adopted a 45-day moratorium on August 26.

In Los Angeles County, Monterey Park voters approved a permanent ban on June 2, making it the first US city to ban data centers outright; the developer had already withdrawn. In Santa Clara, finished data centers built by Digital Realty and Stack have sat empty waiting for Silicon Valley Power to finish a $450 million grid upgrade due in 2028.

On September 21 Gov. Gavin Newsom signed seven bills that make data centers pay for the grid upgrades they cause and disclose expected water use to local governments. Indio's council was scheduled to take up its permanent ban in September; no result has been published, and its moratorium runs through October 16.

Arizona has 16 data center projects proposed or under construction, most of them in Maricopa County, and the newest local limits are in the south of the state. On September 22 Pima County supervisors voted 3-2 for a 120-day moratorium on new data centers in unincorporated areas while the county writes zoning rules. It does not apply to Project Blue near the county fairgrounds or the proposed Project Gravel south of Tucson. In Pinal County, supervisors voted 4-1 on August 26 to reject Vermaland's La Osa Energy Center outside Eloy.

In the West Valley, Maricopa County supervisors voted 4-1 in May to issue a military compatibility permit for Project Baccara, a 160-acre campus with its own 700-megawatt gas power plant about a mile north of Luke Air Force Base, near Surprise and Glendale. The county received 553 emails opposing it and five in support. "You can't drink data, you can't eat data," said Hollie Tolmachoff, who lives less than half a mile away. The project still needs county and federal air quality approval.

Cities are writing their own rules. Tucson's council voted 6-1 on August 5 to require a half-mile buffer from homes and schools, a 50-foot height limit and a public review for any data center over 25,000 square feet or 20 megawatts. Chandler's council voted 7-0 in December 2025 against Active Infrastructure's data center rezoning, despite lobbying by former Sen. Kyrsten Sinema.

Statewide, a three-year pause on new data center sales tax breaks took effect July 1 and runs until June 30, 2029; the state received 113 applications in the two weeks before the deadline, AZPM reported. Pima County's moratorium runs 120 days, into late January 2027, and can be extended.

New York has stopped issuing state environmental permits for new data centers that can use 50 megawatts of power or more. Gov. Kathy Hochul's Executive Order 62, signed July 14, holds them for about a year while the state studies what these projects do to the grid, water and air. Smaller projects, and those that need only local approvals, still go through town boards.

The biggest test is in Massena, in St. Lawrence County, where North Country Collocation Services wants to build a 1.5 million-square-foot campus near the St. Lawrence River that would use about 400 megawatts from the New York Power Authority. The company says the state pause does not cover it. On September 16 the town board voted 3-2 against a six-month local moratorium, with Supervisor Raymond Lancto and Kristy Baker in the minority. "We need a moratorium," said Marina Johnson Zafiris of Akwesasne, whose group, Mohawks United in Safety and Health, leads the opposition.

Niagara County has the most tracked sites, most of them already running, including TeraWulf's Lake Mariner campus in Barker and data centers in North Tonawanda and Niagara Falls, where Niagara Falls Redevelopment has proposed a Niagara Digital Campus. Manhattan's are older buildings such as 60 Hudson Street and 111 Eighth Avenue. Near Syracuse, more than 350 people turned out against Ranalli's proposed 300-megawatt data center in Lysander, and the town passed a six-month moratorium on May 7. In the Town of Tonawanda, hundreds opposed a 300-megawatt campus on the former Tonawanda Coke site.

In Rockland County, Orangetown passed a moratorium in August but exempted DataBank's planned expansion in Orangeburg to 45 megawatts, just under the state's line. A bill from State Sen. Kristen Gonzalez that would extend the pause to data centers as small as 20 megawatts passed in June; Hochul has not committed to signing it. Lysander's moratorium runs out November 7.

Indianapolis has stopped approving new data centers. The Metropolitan Development Commission voted 6-0 on August 19, 2026 to put a moratorium on new data center projects in Marion County through the end of 2027, after the City-County Council passed it 23-1 on August 10. Three projects approved earlier are exempt and still going ahead: Sabey Data Centers' campus in Decatur Township, Metrobloks' $500 million data center in Martindale-Brightwood, and DC Blox's $2 billion campus on a former Ford plant site near Irvington.

Much of the state is moving the same way. By the middle of 2026, Indiana University's Environmental Resilience Institute counted 11 counties with data center ordinances, at least 17 with temporary moratoriums, and two, Marshall and Cass, that have banned new data centers altogether. In Boone County, home to Meta's $10 billion data center in Lebanon, commissioners unanimously approved a one-year moratorium in the unincorporated county on June 15, 2026; it runs through June 15, 2027. Jeffersonville's city council approved a one-year pause on August 3, after New Albany passed one in July.

Councilor Michael-Paul Hart, the only Indianapolis council vote against the pause, said it would leave officials less prepared to deal with developers: "In 2028, there will be a fresh batch of some councilors that are not going to be as educated as the councilors that we have now." While the Indianapolis pause runs, a committee of experts and residents is to study campus size, building height, environmental impacts and sound levels before the city writes permanent rules.

North Carolina's biggest data center under construction is Amazon Web Services' $10 billion campus of 20 buildings in the Energy Way Industrial Park near Hamlet, in Richmond County, the largest single investment in the state's history. The sharpest fight is in Stokes County, where a Charlotte developer, Engineered Land Solutions, wants to build Project Delta on 1,845 acres of forest and farmland near Walnut Cove. Commissioners voided the project's rezoning in April, so the developer has to start the approval process over.

Three of five commissioners approved the rezoning in January. "We've been working for 20 years to try to find a revenue stream like this," Commissioner Rick Morris said then; residents sued, and in March Morris finished last of eight candidates in the Republican primary. The board then voided its vote, saying the lawsuit "correctly pointed out flaws that we needed to address." The developer promises 250 to 500 jobs and up to $40 million a year in county taxes, a figure one opponent called "outlandish."

At least 37 towns and counties have paused new data centers, among them Charlotte, Durham, Asheville, Apex, Chatham County, and, since August 17, Yadkin and Alamance counties. Residents have also driven developers away: Energy Storage Solutions withdrew a $19.2 billion project near Tarboro in Edgecombe County in July as the county weighed a moratorium, and a proposal in southeast Raleigh ended in August after residents filled all 30 comment slots at its hearing. Elsewhere, Microsoft is building two campuses in Catawba County.

State lawmakers have passed no data center rules. The House approved Senate Bill 730, which would make large data centers pay the cost of serving them, 69-44 in June, but the Senate parked it in its Rules Committee, and lawmakers are not expected to take meaningful votes until after the November 3 election, if at all this session.

Missouri's largest data center projects are on an Interstate 70 megasite near New Florence in Montgomery County, where Amazon Data Services and Google are building on nearly 2,000 acres. Amazon's project is north of the highway; Google announced a $15 billion data center south of it in May 2026. Nine towns and counties have paused or banned new data centers, and the next pause to run out is Springfield's 120-day moratorium on October 27.

Montgomery County commissioners approved tax breaks for Amazon in December 2025. The county's own analysis gives Amazon personal property tax exemptions of 75% to 95% from 2028 to 2052, worth $244 million to $982 million, and for Google commissioners planned a 70% break on servers and equipment in return for $10 million a year for 20 years. Residents sued the commission in February under the Sunshine Law over notice of meetings. When residents asked in May why the projects never went to a public vote, Presiding Commissioner Ryan Poston said, "That's not how this works."

Elsewhere, residents have won. The St. Charles City Council voted 7-1 in May to make its one-year moratorium permanent, effectively banning large data centers in the city, after CRG Cumulus withdrew a $1 billion proposal off Highway 370. Festus voters removed four council members in April after the council approved a data center. In Kansas City, the plan commission voted 6-0 on August 5 against a 20-story data center on a historic downtown building after 55 people testified and 475 letters came in against it.

Power bills are the other fight. Ameren Missouri has asked the Public Service Commission for about $343 million more a year, roughly $13 a month for a typical household, while projecting sales to rise more than 60% in five years on new large users such as data centers. State Rep. Brad Christ asked the commission on September 14 to reject the increase: "I get the same bill my neighbors do." The commission is still reviewing the case, file ER-2026-0291, and is taking public comments.

England's largest data center project under way is QTS's campus at Cambois, on the former Blyth Power Station site in Northumberland. Northumberland County Council approved the first two buildings in December 2025, and plans for two more buildings were lodged by early September 2026. Nearby, OpenAI paused its Stargate UK plan at Cobalt Park in North Tyneside in April 2026, citing "regulation and the cost of energy." No planning application had been filed for the site at the time. On August 28 the national government refused calls for a moratorium on large new data centers.

The sharpest local fight is on London's eastern edge, where Digital Reef proposes the East Havering Data Centre Campus on 99 acres of green belt on Fenn Lane in North Ockendon. Havering Council consulted from March 6 to April 7, 2026, on a Local Development Order that would permit it, and the campaign group Protect the Green Belt (North Ockendon Alliance) has threatened a court challenge. "I bought my house here because it was quiet and out in the green fields," one resident told the Havering Daily. The council has not yet published a decision on adopting the order.

Residents have won once in court. In January 2026 the government admitted it had wrongly approved Greystoke Land's data center at Woodlands Park, near Iver in Buckinghamshire, after Buckinghamshire Council refused it and the campaign group Foxglove sued; the approval is to be quashed. Greystoke also won permission on appeal for a data center near Abbots Langley in Hertfordshire after Three Rivers District Council refused it.

Michigan's largest data center, a $43 billion campus for Oracle and OpenAI being developed by Related Digital in Saline Township, Washtenaw County, is being built after the township, under threat of a lawsuit, approved the rezoning it had first denied. A resident has asked the State Tax Commission to reject the project's property tax break, arguing the township skipped a required public hearing. In Van Buren Township, Wayne County, Google's 1-gigawatt Project Cannoli won preliminary site plan approval in February, and its substation was approved in May.

About 50 townships, cities and counties now have a pause or ban on new data centers in force. Residents have also stopped projects outright: Augusta Township voters overturned a data center rezoning in August, about 90 percent to 10, and Allen Park's planning commission voted 7-2 against a 26-megawatt data center near homes and a high school. Developers withdrew in Howell Township, Lansing and Washington Township in Macomb County.

Microsoft has plans in Gaines and Lowell townships in Kent County and in Dorr Township in Allegan County. Its Lowell Township project is on hold while the township writes a data center ordinance. "We cannot just exclude Microsoft. That's exclusionary law in the state of Michigan," said Julie Echtinaw, who lives across the street from the site and sits on the committee drafting it. In Ypsilanti Township, officials oppose a University of Michigan and Los Alamos National Laboratory data center on 124 wooded acres, but the university is exempt from local zoning.

Gov. Gretchen Whitmer's plan, released in July, asks data center companies to sign a voluntary pledge to cover their own costs and asks lawmakers to write consumer protections into law; her office has said she would veto a statewide moratorium.

Oregon's data centers are concentrated in two places: Hillsboro, west of Portland, and Morrow and Umatilla counties around Boardman and Hermiston, where Amazon runs or is building most of them. Amazon bought more than 1,000 acres near Boardman this year for what it calls its Exascale Project, which a local organizer says would use a gigawatt of electricity. Hillsboro has a 120-day moratorium on new data center approvals, passed unanimously in July and set to end November 23.

In Morrow County the fight is over drinking water. In March Amazon agreed to pay $20.5 million, without admitting fault, to settle a lawsuit by residents whose wells are contaminated with nitrate; the Port of Morrow spreads wastewater from food processors and data centers on farm fields. The Oregon Health Authority has found at least 634 wells in the area with unsafe nitrate levels. The residents are still suing the port and other defendants and are seeking class-action status.

In Washington County, candidates who campaigned against data centers won Democratic primaries in May, and teachers and conservation groups are suing the county and Hillsboro over a string of data center tax breaks. In Salem, Gov. Tina Kotek canceled a state land sale to Verrus in July, though its 75-acre campus is still under city review. At The Dalles, where Google runs data centers, OPB found Google's water use grew from 104 million gallons in 2012 to 434 million in 2024.

Since July, Portland General Electric's data center customers pay 29% more under a 2025 state law, while household rates fell 1.3%. Four Democratic lawmakers plan to propose a three-year moratorium on new large data centers when the Legislature meets in January.

Iowa's sharpest data center fight is in Salix, a town of about 300 in Woodbury County that annexed about 900 acres of farmland in April for a possible data center. MidAmerican Energy named Google as the prospective customer on August 3, and on August 20 the city council voted 3-2 against a one-year moratorium. The council has started drafting data center rules and put off a data center memorandum of understanding until its October 14 meeting.

Nothing can be built yet. The land would still need rezoning, and Woodbury County and several landowners are challenging the annexation in court, arguing Salix did not notify neighbors properly and took in land that does not touch the town. County supervisors voted 5-0 on June 23 for a one-year moratorium in unincorporated areas; State Sen. Kevin Alons of Salix told them MidAmerican had evaded questions about the project's size. "Whatever you guys do will affect us," Winnebago Tribe of Nebraska council member Keely Bassette Purscell told the Salix council.

The state's largest project is QTS's seven-building, 612-acre campus at the Big Cedar Industrial Center in Cedar Rapids, projected at $10 billion, where business leaders said 8,500 people were working in April. QTS says it will use a closed-loop cooling system, and QTS and Alliant Energy promised existing customers a five-year electricity rate freeze that ends in 2030. Linn County supervisors voted 2-1 on July 1 for an 18-month moratorium in unincorporated areas. Dubuque County approved a 12-month pause on May 26 after land south of Dubuque was bought for a possible data center.

Iowa Citizens for Community Improvement counts more than 25 counties and at least six cities with some form of pause and is urging more. Unions and economic development groups have formed Growing Iowa's Economy to promote what they call "responsible development" of data centers.

Frankfurt is one of Europe's largest data center hubs, and it has run out of grid power for new ones: operators have already secured all the capacity available, according to Max Kendl of the Frankfurt Chamber of Industry and Commerce. The grid company NRM, part of Mainova, still gets five to 10 serious requests a year from data center builders, each for 50 to 100 megawatts. Since 2022 the city has limited new data centers to seven zones, so new projects are moving out to smaller towns around Frankfurt.

Two of those towns have said no this year. On February 3, 2026, Groß-Gerau's council voted 18-14 against negotiating with Vantage Data Centers over a 174-megawatt, €2.5 billion campus in the Lausböhl industrial park. "We will not sell our city of Groß-Gerau to a multi-billion-dollar investor," said SPD leader Susanne Theisen-Canibol. In July, STACK Infrastructure pulled out of a €3 billion data center on the former Continental site in Babenhausen after the council majority demanded renewable power, noise limits, a water plan and a €250 million guarantee. The landowner, Aumovio, is now looking for a new investor.

Where the grid cannot deliver, some builders are making their own power. CyrusOne is covering the expansion of its FRA7 data center on the Frankfurt Westside campus from 84 to 126 megawatts with gas-fired generators run with the energy company EON. "This is not an isolated case, but one that occurs frequently in the Frankfurt area," said Marina Köhn of the Federal Environment Agency. Approval for such plants usually comes from Hesse's regional councils.

Australia has 162 data centers operating and about 90 more in the pipeline, according to the industry group Data Centres Australia. The biggest proposal is NEXTDC's S7 campus at Eastern Creek in Sydney's western suburbs: nine buildings with 612 megawatts of power, with OpenAI signed up to use part of it. NEXTDC filed the plans in March; like every large project in New South Wales, it will be decided by the state government, not the local council.

The sharpest local fight was in Lane Cove West, where Goodman Group proposed Project Mars at 12 Mars Road, a 90-megawatt data center running around the clock about 160 meters from a primary school. It drew 374 submissions, 358 of them objections, and the New South Wales planning portal now lists it as withdrawn. In neighboring Macquarie Park, where five data centers operate and six more are proposed, Ryde Mayor Trenton Brown said: "Local councils were effectively cut out of the planning process."

Two other proposals were pulled this year after residents objected. GreenSquareDC withdrew its 120-megawatt Hazelmere data center near Perth on May 14, after almost 1,900 public submissions and a City of Swan staff report recommending refusal. MAK Urban Group withdrew its data center in North Katoomba, in the Blue Mountains, in June, after a petition with more than 730 signatures.

On August 26, 2026, the federal, state and territory governments agreed on mandatory national standards that will require large data centers to add at least as much energy to the grid as they draw and to limit their water use. The legislation is due in early 2027.

Singapore's next data centers will be on Jurong Island, the man-made island that holds the petroleum and chemical plants. On August 21, 2026, the Economic Development Board and the Infocomm Media Development Authority gave 50 megawatts of power each to Digital Realty, Equinix, Keppel and ST Telemedia Global Data Centers (STT GDC), chosen from more than 20 proposals. The sites will sit in a low-carbon data center park being built by the state agency JTC; Keppel says its share will go to a S$1 billion building, Keppel DC SGP 11.

Singapore halted new data centers in 2019 and now hands out power in rounds instead of letting companies build freely. The conditions are strict: half of each site's power must come from low-carbon sources such as biomethane, ammonia or hydrogen, and all four winners will use liquid cooling. An earlier round in 2023 gave 80 megawatts to Equinix, GDS, Microsoft and a group of AirTrunk and ByteDance. The government says it will decide in 18 to 24 months whether to hold another round.

Existing sites are being expanded too. Keppel began building a 25-megawatt floating data center at 25 Loyang Crescent in 2026, cooled with seawater and due to go live in 2028, and planned to start the third building at its Genting Lane campus in mid-2026.

Britain's data center fights are mostly in the green belt around London, and ministers have usually sided with the builders. In May 2025 the government overturned Three Rivers District Council's refusal of Greystoke Land's 96-megawatt, £1 billion data center off Bedmond Road near Abbots Langley, Hertfordshire, saying investment could otherwise go to markets outside the UK. Months earlier it had approved a 140-megawatt scheme at the Court Lane Industrial Estate in Buckinghamshire that local officials had rejected.

Opponents have won some. In January 2026 the government conceded a High Court challenge by the campaign group Foxglove and agreed to quash its approval of Greystoke's Woodlands Park data center near Iver, which Buckinghamshire Council had refused. "It shouldn't take us having to drag the government to court," said Foxglove's Rosa Curling.

The biggest project under way is QTS's campus at Cambois in Northumberland, on the former Blyth Power Station site. Northumberland Council approved the first phase in December 2025, and QTS said it would install piling for the first building in spring 2026. OpenAI paused its Stargate UK project at Cobalt Park in North Tyneside in April 2026, citing regulation and energy costs.

Outside England, Edinburgh's council unanimously refused a 210-megawatt data center on the city's outskirts in February 2026, and the Scottish Government has put the developer's appeal on hold until it produces a full environmental assessment. Anglesey refused a data center on the old Octel chemical site at Amlwch in April 2026.

National policy keeps pushing for more. A revised National Planning Policy Framework for England, published August 17, 2026, strengthens support for data centers, and on August 28 the government rejected the Green Party's call for a moratorium on large new ones, saying a pause would push investment and jobs overseas.

China's biggest data center cluster is in Ulanqab, a windy city in Inner Mongolia northwest of Beijing that sells itself on cheap power. On August 6, 2026, Envision Group opened its Envision Galaxy Campus there, which it calls China's largest AI computing park, planned for 2 gigawatts of power with more than 80 percent of its electricity from directly connected renewable sources. DeepSeek, the Hangzhou AI company, is planning its own 1-gigawatt data center in Ulanqab and aims to bring part of it online by the end of 2027 or early 2028, Bloomberg reported.

More than a dozen companies have projects planned in Ulanqab, according to a compilation of local government approvals cited by Bloomberg. Local officials say data takes 4.2 milliseconds to travel from Beijing. "When electricity is cheap, tokens are cheap," Zhang Xiaorong of the Cutting-Edge Technology Research Institute told the Global Times, adding that this gives Ulanqab "a significant advantage." The table below also lists Huawei, Alibaba, Apple and VNET sites in Ulanqab and nearby Hohhot, and Tencent and Huawei campuses across the country, from Gui'an in Guizhou to Qingyuan in Guangdong.

Much of what China has built sits idle. After local governments competed to back data centers, the government estimated utilization at around 20 to 30 percent, and more than 100 state-backed data center projects were canceled in 18 months, Reuters reported in 2025. The Ministry of Industry and Information Technology is working with China Mobile, China Unicom and China Telecom on a national platform to sell the surplus computing power, with common connection standards expected by 2028.

Most of Germany's data centers are around Frankfurt, one of Europe's largest hubs, and the towns around it are now deciding whether to take more. Three proposals were stopped this year. Groß-Gerau's council voted 18-14 in February against negotiating with Vantage over a 174-megawatt, 2.5 billion euro campus; STACK Infrastructure dropped a 3 billion euro plan in Babenhausen in July; and on July 2 Eisenach's city council, in Thuringia, stopped a data center planned for 80 hectares of farmland near Stockhausen.

In Eisenach, 19 council members backed a residents' petition to keep the farmland and 16 opposed it, while about 60 people protested outside. The petition's organizer, Steffi Wiegand, said she expects the mayor to bring the plan back and that her group will be ready. In Babenhausen, southeast of Frankfurt, a council coalition had demanded more renewable power, a noise cap, other cooling options and a 250 million euro guarantee; the landowner, Aumovio, blamed "protracted and uncertain processes."

Other projects are moving ahead, including NTT's approved campus at Nierstein on the Rhine, Microsoft's sites at Bergheim and Elsdorf west of Cologne, and Amazon Web Services' plans in Brandenburg, all listed below. Under the federal Energy Efficiency Act, any data center that opens from July 1, 2026 must reuse at least 10 percent of its energy as waste heat, rising to 20 percent for those opening in 2028.

India's biggest data center project is Google's $15 billion, 1-gigawatt AI hub around Visakhapatnam in Andhra Pradesh, built with AdaniConneX and Airtel's Nxtra. Google broke ground on April 28, 2026 at Tarluvada, a village of about 3,000 people in Anandapuram mandal, which holds the main 266.6-acre site; two more sites are planned on 174.8 acres at Rambilli in Anakapalli district and 160 acres at Adavivaram-Mudasarlova. The project is to be built over five years.

Most of the Tarluvada land was farmed. About 204 of the 308.657 acres the state allotted to Google were assigned or unrecorded land held by farmers. After farmers asked, the state raised compensation to ₹20 lakh an acre for assigned land and ₹10 lakh for unrecorded land, plus 3 cents of house-site land per family; farmers asked for 5 cents. People in the area worry about groundwater in a region that is already short of water, Business Standard reported.

The other fight is in Thane, outside Mumbai, where Amazon Web Services plans a campus of about 53 acres at Balkum and Majiwada. Residents began protesting when they learned it had been classed as an essential service, giving it priority for water and power, and formed a campaign, Wake Up Thanekar, to demand public consultation. Answering local MP Naresh Mhaske's call to halt construction, Amazon said on July 8, 2026 that its tree felling had a city permit and the site would not use drinking water for cooling.

Brazil's biggest new data center, and its most contested, is a campus inside the Pecém Industrial and Port Complex north of Fortaleza, in Ceará, being developed by the wind power company Casa dos Ventos to be run by TikTok's parent company, ByteDance. Plans show 210 megawatts of power in the first phase and up to 300 at full build-out, with operations scheduled for January 2027 and up to 50 billion reais, about $8.7 billion, in investment. Most of the other data centers listed below are around São Paulo, in Barueri, Santana de Parnaíba, Hortolândia, Campinas and Vinhedo.

The Anace Indigenous community, which lives around Caucaia and São Gonçalo do Amarante, says the Pecém campus is on land it claims. It occupied the Caucaia offices of SEMACE, the state environment agency, on August 4, 2025, and on August 26 filed a complaint seeking to cancel the environmental license, arguing the project was wrongly classed as low-impact. Casa dos Ventos says the work is more than 20 kilometers from Indigenous territory; Anace leader Cacique Roberto Ytaysaba Anace puts it at 3 kilometers.
The complaint also disputes the company's figure of about 30,000 liters of water a day. Casa dos Ventos says the campus will use closed-loop liquid cooling, which uses less water than older systems.

On September 15, 2026, President Lula signed a law creating ReData, which suspends import and federal taxes on data center equipment for up to five years. In return, companies must keep at least 10 percent of their capacity for the Brazilian market and meet renewable-power and water-efficiency rules. The House passed the bill in February under an urgent procedure, without committee review, and the Senate passed it on September 1.

Most of Japan's data centers are around Tokyo and Osaka, and the newest fight is on Tokyo's western edge. In Hino, residents oppose a large data center planned near their homes. "This is a terrible plan," Yoriko Kitagawa, 94, told AFP, and on June 30, 2026 neighbors put up protest flags reading "Do Not Push Forward with the Data Center Construction!" Nearby in Fuchu, DayOne and Gaw Capital have broken ground on an 80-megawatt campus in Fuchu Intelligent Park; its first nine-story building is due by mid-2027.

The biggest cluster east of Tokyo is in Inzai, Chiba, where Equinix, MC Digital Realty, STACK and AirTrunk have sites; near Osaka, data centers gather in the Keihanna science city and in Ibaraki. Power and builders are the limits. Yasuo Suzuki of NTT Global Data Centers says developers around Tokyo face long waits for power, and may wait up to three years just to start construction because contractors are fully booked.

Meta is planning a $13 billion data center complex in Sturgeon County, north of Edmonton, announced in July 2026. Hundreds of people protested outside the county office in August. Alberta's grid operator says it can connect only 1.2 gigawatts of new data center load by 2028, and it gave that to two of the 36 projects that had applied, pausing the rest.

In August the Alberta Utilities Commission rejected the gas plant behind Synapse Real Estate Corp.'s data center campus in Olds, Alberta, which would have generated 1.4 gigawatts. "The project is too close to the surrounding community," the commission said, noting the site was about 30 meters from the first row of homes. Rocky View County, near Calgary, stopped bringing data center rezonings to council on July 21 while it writes new rules. Oakville, Ontario, adopted a one-year moratorium in August.

Other provinces are rationing power. British Columbia is making 400 megawatts available over two years from February 2026, with no project getting more than 145. Hydro-Québec has asked to charge large data centers 13 cents a kilowatt-hour, about double what other large power customers pay.

Amazon Web Services' plan for a data center on 600 acres in Madison and St. Clair townships, Butler County, Ohio, is on hold until after the Nov. 3 election. The City of Trenton withdrew its annexation petition in September 2026, a day before a county commission hearing, after both townships denied the request and Amazon offered each township $5 million plus property taxes. "To me, what's the factor is you're losing your democracy," said St. Clair Township landowner Joe Krueger, who says he will not sell. Trenton voters decide on Election Day whether to ban data centers above 25 megawatts; if Amazon instead goes through Madison Township, the county commission would decide.

In Tucson, Arizona, the city council voted 7-0 on Aug. 6, 2025 to end talks on Project Blue, a data center campus near the Pima County Fairgrounds, after meetings drew crowds of 800 to 1,000 people over its water use. Beale Infrastructure had been the public face of the project until Amazon's involvement was accidentally released to Arizona Luminaria. The project went ahead without the city: Pima County sold the land to Beale for more than $27 million on Dec. 24, 2025, and construction began in April 2026, when dozens of protesters tried to block trucks at the site.

In Missouri, Amazon and Google are building data centers on a combined 1,900 acres east of New Florence, in Montgomery County. The advocacy group Preserve Montgomery County sued the county and the state in February 2026, arguing officials gave inadequate public notice about the data centers' water and electricity use and a tax abatement. In September 2026 a Cole County judge refused to dismiss most of the suit, ruling the group has standing; the case against Montgomery County can now go forward.

Meta's biggest fight is over the power plants for its Richland Parish campus in northern Louisiana. In April 2026 Entergy Louisiana asked state regulators to approve seven more gas-fired power plants for the campus, on top of three already approved, for ten plants of 754 megawatts of power each, serving this one customer. The Union of Concerned Scientists said that is enough power to meet New Orleans' peak demand six times over. The Public Service Commission's final decision on the seven plants is scheduled for December 16, 2026.

Entergy broke ground on the first two plants, the roughly 1.5-gigawatt Franklin Farms Power Station, for a campus first announced at about $10 billion. Meta offered to pay those plants' full annual revenue for 15 years, but environmental groups say Entergy did not choose the most cost-effective option for ratepayers. Regulators killed a subpoena on August 12, 2026, already upheld by a judge, that would have made Meta document its investment, jobs and power demand; in December 2025 they had adopted a rule fast-tracking approval of power plants built mainly for data centers, requiring those customers to pay half the cost.

At Meta's campus in Huntsville, Alabama, construction is under way on two more buildings that will expand it to about 2.5 million square feet; a meeting with city leaders in August 2026 drew questions about its water and power use, noise and jobs, and a residents' group there wants a moratorium on new data centers. In Temple, Texas, residents urged the Bell County Commissioners Court in July 2026 to stop giving data centers tax abatements, pointing to the ones Meta already holds from both the city and the county.

Microsoft's Fairwater AI data center in Mount Pleasant, Wisconsin, is facing a class action lawsuit from neighbors over noise. Three residents of neighboring Sturtevant sued in federal court in July 2026, saying the fans on the 1.2 million square foot campus "physically invade" nearby properties; they want to represent everyone within 1.5 miles, more than 1,000 households. One plaintiff says the noise forced him to move to a later work shift because he could not sleep. Microsoft calls the site an "AI superfactory."

Microsoft has also pulled back elsewhere. Analysts reported in early 2025 that it had canceled US data center leases, then that it had walked away from pending leases in the US and Europe totaling 2 gigawatts, largely because it decided not to support more OpenAI training work; other analysts said Microsoft still had about 5 gigawatts of leased capacity due online through 2028. In September 2026, Bloomberg reported that Microsoft still plans to grow its global footprint from about 12 gigawatts to more than 38 gigawatts of power by 2032. Chief executive Satya Nadella has said the constraint is not chips but having finished buildings ready to fill with computers.
For power, Microsoft has a 20-year deal with Constellation Energy for output from the restarted Three Mile Island reactor in Pennsylvania, due back online in 2028.

In 2026, towns and states across the country started pushing back on data centers. Local opposition blocked more than 75 projects worth about $130 billion in the first four months of the year, and 45 worth $68 billion in the second quarter alone, mostly through county boards and town councils rather than state law.

Texas has gone furthest. On August 3 Governor Greg Abbott halted data center approvals until regulators audit every project waiting to connect to the state grid, and on September 21 he widened the pause to environmental permits. Counties there have less room of their own: Hood County commissioners voted 3-2 against a local moratorium after a state senator wrote that they had no power to pass one.
In New York, the Legislature passed a one-year pause on large data centers on June 4, by 44-16 in the Senate and 102-39 in the Assembly. It takes effect only if Governor Kathy Hochul signs it.
Pick your state below to see what is proposed near you, where residents have already won, and which local pauses are in force.

Fairfax County tightened its data center rules early: on September 10, 2024 the Board of Supervisors adopted a zoning ordinance amendment 8-2, effective the next day, restricting where a data center can go and what it must meet to get there. The county already has nine tracked sites, five of them operating, spread from Tysons to Herndon to Chantilly.

The newest fight is over Starwood's Plaza 500 proposal, a 34-acre data center campus at 6295 and 6299 Edsall Road in Lincolnia, allowed there by right under county zoning. It would sit 67 feet from the nearest home and border a protected area along Turkeycock Run. On August 27, 2026 the Fairfax County Federation of Citizens Associations voted to oppose the project and the roughly five-acre Dominion Energy substation that would power it, citing noise and environmental effects; the substation is expected to carry 176 megawatts.

Opposition to the substation crosses jurisdictions: Representative Don Beyer, Mason District Supervisor Andres Jimenez, Alexandria Mayor Alyia Gaskins and the Alexandria City Council, State Senator Elizabeth Bennett-Parker, House Majority Leader Charniele Herring and Delegate Vivian Watts have all come out against it. The Fairfax County Planning Commission takes up the substation's required public facilities review on December 2, 2026.

Five of the county's nine tracked sites are already operating. Amazon Web Services runs a Mallory Drive facility in Chantilly and is building at Loisdale Station in Springfield and at Renaissance Technology Park in Herndon. CoreSite operates and is expanding its campus on Sunrise Valley Drive in Reston, and Mapletree Industrial Trust runs the Roosevelt Building in McLean.

Digital Realty's VA3 building, on Business Center Drive in Reston, is also running, despite carrying "Manassas" in its record name; Elias DC Assets runs a smaller, 3-megawatt site in Tysons. The one other proposal on record, T5 Data Centers' 60-megawatt campus at Westfields in Chantilly, has not yet broken ground.

Warrenton's town council approved a special use permit for a 220,000-square-foot Amazon data center on Blackwell Road in February 2023, and voters replaced every council member who had backed it in the November 2024 election. The new council, made up entirely of opponents, still faces a 2023 lawsuit by Citizens for Fauquier County over that permit. Both sides argued the case in Fauquier County Circuit Court on June 16, 2026, and Judge Stephen Sincavage has not ruled or set a timetable for a ruling.

The town itself now argues against its own permit. Town attorney Philip Carter Strother told the judge that Warrenton "no longer shares Amazon's litigation alignment," after the council banned data centers from industrial zoning in July 2025, a ban that came too late to stop Amazon's project. Amazon and the plaintiffs also disagree over whether a 30-day deadline to challenge the underlying zoning change has already passed.

Ten other projects are on record around the county. In Remington, PointOne's 300-megawatt Remington Technology Park has been approved, while Gigaland's 800-megawatt campus, Convergent's 240-megawatt campus and SDC Capital's Remington Innovation Campus have all been withdrawn; SAMX Data Center is still proposed. Near Warrenton, CyrusOne and Vint Hill Corners have proposed projects and OVHcloud's Vint Hill facility is operating and expanding. Catlett Data Center Park, in Catlett, was cancelled. No ruling date has been set in the Amazon case.

Stafford County counted 16 data center applications in its pipeline as of a June 23, 2026 board work session: five approved, three of those under construction, and 11 still being reviewed. Under construction now are STACK Stafford, planned for 1,100 megawatts of power, Vantage Fredericksburg at 192 MW, and Amazon's Stafford Potomac Church campus. The county stopped taking new applications after adopting a stricter ordinance and comprehensive plan update in September 2025.

Supervisors and staff have said openly that halting the 11 pending applications mid-review would likely not survive a legal challenge, since Virginia law limits pauses on lawfully submitted applications. The board has instead discussed hiring an outside consultant and building public dashboards so residents can track applications without filing records requests. Approvals have continued anyway: the planning commission voted 4-3 in August to recommend the 590,000-square-foot Accokeek Center near the Rappahannock Regional Jail, and supervisors separately approved the Stafford Technology Center, a 23-building complex projected to generate $127 million a year in tax revenue.

Starting July 1, 2026, Virginia's House Bill 153 requires a sound-profile assessment for any facility of 100 megawatts or more sited near homes or schools, along with details of the substation serving it, so Stafford has to update its zoning ordinance again. The county is also holding public meetings on the comprehensive plan update that will decide where future data centers can go.

CyrusOne, a Dallas-based data center developer owned by the investment firms KKR and BlackRock, put itself in front of county boards and courtrooms on two continents this year. In several places, residents asked the same question: how much say local government actually has.

In Freestone County, Texas, CyrusOne is building a campus beside Calpine's Freestone Energy Center gas plant near Fairfield, with plans for up to 760 megawatts in two phases; the first phase is already under construction. About 30 people spoke against a tax abatement for phase two at a June 10 hearing, worried about noise and water use. Before a follow-up hearing on June 17, CyrusOne withdrew its abatement request and the hearing was cancelled. County Judge Lloyd Lane said that removed the county's only leverage. "The Tax Abatement Agreement was our only way to have any say in what these companies can and cannot do, and now that is off the table," he said. "Texas is a private property rights state."

In Sangamon County, Illinois, the county board approved a roughly 600 megawatt CyrusOne campus on farmland near Waverly on April 7, 2026, by 17 votes to 10. On July 6 farming families, including the Caruthers family, and a neighboring kennel owner sued to overturn the approval. The county asked a judge to dismiss the case, with a hearing set for October 9, 2026. Illinois Times reported that CyrusOne was already talking with county officials in February 2025, before the county wrote its data center zoning rules.

In west London, Ealing Council approved a CyrusOne data center on the former Honey Monster food factory site in Southall on July 15, 2026; the council will receive almost 17.8 million pounds in planning contributions. With the local grid under strain, CyrusOne said it had secured its own electricity supply from elsewhere rather than draw on it.

CyrusOne is also building a five-building, 400 megawatt campus in Whitney, in Bosque County, Texas, next to Calpine's Thad Hill Energy Center. The newest of the five buildings, a $430 million, 93,000 square foot facility called DFW17C, is due to finish by April 2027.

Oracle's name is often the one in headlines, but other companies own most of the land it operates on. Oracle is the cloud tenant, with OpenAI as its customer, on campuses being built by other developers: Crusoe's site in Abilene, Texas; Vantage Data Centers' 1.4 gigawatt Frontier campus in Shackelford County, Texas, and its $15 billion campus in Port Washington, Wisconsin; Related Digital's campus in Saline Township, Michigan; and Project Jupiter in Doña Ana County, New Mexico. As much as $300 billion of OpenAI's projected spending is expected to go to Oracle, which has taken on debt and cut about 21,000 jobs, 13 percent of its workforce, in fiscal 2026 to help fund its share.

In Michigan, Saline Township's board refused to rezone farmland for the Related Digital campus; the developer sued, and the township settled, allowing it to proceed. A judge in February 2026 refused to reopen the case after a resident challenged a closed-session settlement vote, noting the developer had already paid a non-refundable $40 million deposit to the local utility and ordered $2 billion of equipment. Michigan's attorney general has separately moved to reopen the utility's fast-tracked approval of the project's power contracts, calling it "the Oracle/Open AI boondoggle."

In New Mexico, county commissioners pledged $165 billion in industrial revenue bonds for Project Jupiter after a closed meeting in September 2025, and a lawsuit alleges that meeting broke the state's open-meetings law. Construction has continued regardless; Oracle told the county commission in September 2026 that the site was already 26 percent built, with about 3,500 workers on site.

In Texas, Abilene gave the Stargate campus an 85 percent tax break in exchange for an estimated $30 million a year in other tax revenue and thousands of jobs, but the influx of workers has driven local rents up sharply. Oracle and OpenAI have since dropped a planned expansion there. Oracle has not said how much power or water its Stargate campuses will use in total.

Johor is where Malaysia's data center boom is concentrated, with 15 of the country's 26 tracked projects. YTL Power runs 600 megawatts of operating capacity at its Kulai park, and STACK Infrastructure is building a 220-megawatt campus in two buildings at Iskandar Puteri, due to start delivering space in late 2026. AirTrunk opened its first Johor Bahru site in 2024 and plans two more facilities, JHB3 and JHB4, adding more than 280 megawatts. On February 24, 2026, Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim said Malaysia had stopped accepting new applications for data centers that are not built for artificial intelligence, citing pressure on power and water.

Water use is the flashpoint. AirTrunk says its planned JHB3 and JHB4 will run on recycled water. In August 2026, YTL and JLand announced a separate gigawatt-scale campus at Sedenak Tech Park West, next to YTL's existing Kulai park. Thirteen of the tracked Malaysian projects, including several large Johor sites, do not have a public construction status yet.

Selangor has the country's other big cluster: Vantage Data Centers is building a 436-megawatt campus at Cyberjaya, and Google is building a 100-megawatt site at Elmina Business Park. In July 2026, a proposed data center in Petaling Jaya's Kota Damansara was withdrawn by its developer after residents objected.

Digital Realty rents data center space to other companies and has been in the business long enough that many of its fights are in cities rather than farmland. Its best known Chicago building, at 350 East Cermak Road, was a printing plant built around 1912 that now covers 1.1 million square feet with 109 megawatts of capacity, used by hundreds of companies including Zoom. On the vacant lot next door, at 21st Street and Calumet Avenue in the South Loop, Digital Realty has proposed a $500 million, 13-story, 565,069 square foot data center joined to Cermak by a bridge.

Residents who already live with noise and soot from the Cermak building oppose the new one. "We have many examples of years of bad acting from Digital Realty, and they don't deserve the opportunity to put up another data center," said Tina Feldstein of the Prairie District Neighborhood Alliance. Neighbors had collected about 680 signatures against the plan by September 2023. At the company's older building at 600 South Federal Street, the city's health department found rooftop generators exceeded the noise ordinance in 2021 and fined Digital Realty $300; the company later built a 15-foot sound wall.

In Atlanta, Digital Realty wants to build a $500 million data center at 713 Ralph David Abernathy Boulevard, where the West End, Adair Park and Mechanicsville neighborhoods meet, within a five-minute walk of a MARTA station. Atlanta has banned data centers within half a mile of MARTA stations since 2024; a council member has proposed an amendment allowing them under conditions. In April a neighborhood planning unit voted 105 to 87 against the change, and in July the Zoning Review Board upheld the ban. The City Council is holding the amendment with no date set.

At an August 3 council meeting, resident Norma Harris said, "Once we have it in a neighborhood, any neighborhood, you can't take it away." Community advocate Tyrone Clemons called it "redlining 2.0," saying large developments by private interests keep landing in predominantly Black areas. Digital Realty has offered $10 million in community investment.

Inner Mongolia holds one of China's biggest concentrations of data centers, in two cities: Hohhot, the regional capital, and Ulanqab, about 240 kilometers from Beijing. The largest single site is Envision Group's Envision Galaxy Campus in Ulanqab, which began operating on August 6, 2026 and is planned for 2 gigawatts of power. The next big one is DeepSeek's: the Chinese AI company is planning a data center of about 1 gigawatt in Ulanqab, hoping to bring part of it online by the end of 2027 or early 2028, Bloomberg reported in July.

The region sells cold weather and wind and solar power. Officials say more than 85% of the electricity its data centers use is green power, and electricity is 60 to 70% of a data center's running costs, according to Cao Zhanwei, who heads the enterprise service center in Hohhot's Horinger New Area. By July 2026 the region counted about one-seventh of China's computing power.

The Hohhot-Ulanqab cluster has drawn China's major phone carriers, big technology companies and state financial institutions, officials say. Ulanqab also hosts Apple's second data center in China, and more than a dozen firms have projects planned in the city, according to a compilation of local government approvals cited by Bloomberg. Envision's campus covers 120,000 square meters, about 20 soccer fields, and the company says more than 80% of its power comes directly from renewable sources. It is the first of 5 gigawatts of desert data centers Envision plans worldwide by 2030.

Most of Spain's new data centers are planned in Aragon, around Zaragoza, where about 30 projects are moving through approvals and more than €47 billion has been committed. The largest single plan is Blackstone's Campus Rhodes at Calatorao, up to eight data centers and 650 megawatts of power. The next decision is national: on August 26, 2026, the Spanish cabinet sent out a draft royal decree that would make data centers of 1 megawatt or more match at least 80% of their power use, hour by hour, with new renewable generation.

Regional governments are fighting the decree. Aragon's economy minister, Eva Valle, called it "especially damaging" for the region, and Madrid's government, which counts 56 projects in its own pipeline, asked for it to be withdrawn. The public comment period closed on September 4; no final decree has been published. Government sources said the rule is "in no case" a moratorium.

Opponents in Aragon object to fast-tracking. In August 2026 the regional environmental agency, INAGA, cleared Campus Rhodes through a simplified environmental review instead of the full one, and Ecologistas en Acción has filed objections against projects being declared strategic for the region. In Catalonia, a campaign backed by more than 140 organizations protested outside the AI Summit Barcelona, demanding a moratorium on data centers over 5 megawatts. The Catalan city of Lleida has banned data centers outright.

Water is the argument in Talavera de la Reina, Toledo province, where Meta plans a €1.1 billion data center. The Tagus basin authority warned that early projections showed 665.4 million liters of drinking water a year; Meta cut its plan by 24%, and the regional government has called the expected use "adequate" for the area.

xAI is the artificial intelligence company Elon Musk founded in 2023; its flagship product is Grok, a chatbot built into the social platform X. It builds its own giant training clusters, mostly in and around Memphis, Tennessee. It announced the first, which became Colossus 1, in Memphis in June 2024, and in March 2025 it said it would build a second data center, Colossus 2, on Tulane Road in the Whitehaven neighborhood. The research group Epoch AI now lists the chips at Colossus 2 as owned by SpaceXAI and estimates the site draws about 946MW of IT power, rising to about 1,531MW by early 2027.

The company has also spread across the state line. In January 2026 Mississippi's governor announced a third data center, called MACROHARDRR, in a warehouse xAI bought in Southaven, as an investment of more than $20 billion, the largest in the state's history; Musk said it would push his Colossus training compute to about 2 gigawatts. On July 29, 2026 Musk said xAI was building a fourth, Minihard, next to Colossus 2 and the Macro-harder site on Tulane Road, with the same 220,000 GB300 chips in a denser layout. Away from Memphis, xAI and X share a cluster of about 12,448 Nvidia GPUs and $700 million of equipment inside a data center in Atlanta, financed through Develop Fulton.

Power is the fight at every Memphis site. xAI ran gas turbines at Colossus 1 without permits until mid-2025, removing them after the law center sent a notice of intent to sue; the Shelby County Health Department then permitted 15, and in December 2025 the local air board dismissed an appeal of that permit 6 to 1 as moot. To run Colossus 2 quickly, xAI installed turbines at the former Duke Energy plant on Stanton Road in Southaven. On April 14, 2026 the NAACP, represented by the Southern Environmental Law Center and Earthjustice, sued xAI and its subsidiary MZX Tech in federal district court in northern Mississippi, saying 27 turbines were running there without an air permit, and in May it asked for a preliminary injunction after the count rose to 33. Mississippi's environmental regulator approved a permanent plant of 41 turbines in March 2026. Residents have also filed a class action over turbine noise.

In July 2026 SpaceXAI said it would remove all 69 turbines at the Stanton Road site between August 2026 and July 2027 and replace them with a permanent 1.2-gigawatt plant, under state rules that bar new turbines after July 15. The law center said the company had added nine turbines that month. Meanwhile Colossus 1 has a new tenant: in May 2026 Anthropic said it would use all of that data center's capacity, more than 300MW. Mississippi's Department of Environmental Quality oversees that removal, with a retirement date set for each turbine and legal action possible for non-compliance.

Aligned Data Centers lost a fight in Ohio in August 2026, when Pataskala City Council voted to block its planned 200-megawatt, three-building campus in the Pataskala Corporate Park, Licking County, after a meeting that ran more than three hours. The city's planning and zoning commission had already voted 5-2 to recommend denial. "There was big concerns with the power alone," Council President Brandon Galik said after the unanimous vote. Pataskala voters decide on Nov. 3 whether to ban large data centers outright. Aligned, based in Dallas, runs 51 campuses across the Americas with more than 6.4 GW of operating and planned capacity; a consortium including BlackRock's Global Infrastructure Partners and the Abu Dhabi investor MGX bought the company from Macquarie Asset Management for $40 billion.

In Maryland, Aligned is building four buildings on Quantum Frederick, the former Alcoa Eastalco aluminum plant site south of Frederick. Its first attempt stalled when regulators denied its backup-generator permits, but after a 2024 state law exempted those generators, it returned and broke ground on the first building in February 2025. Frederick County residents gathered more than 21,000 signatures for a referendum on the county's data center zoning, but Maryland's Supreme Court upheld a ruling against putting it to a vote. County Executive Jessica Fitzwater has since paused new data center approvals until Dec. 31, 2026, though the pause does not cover Quantum Frederick, which was already approved.

Its largest project is Project Phoenix, a 2 GW campus in the Shippingport Industrial Park, Beaver County, Pennsylvania, on the site of the former Bruce Mansfield coal plant. Aligned broke ground there on Sept. 10 and says the campus will draw power from a dedicated on-site source rather than the local grid. "I feel they're popping up everywhere like Dollar General stores," said Jai-Ellen St. George of Midland. In Ohio, Aligned is also building NEO-01, a 96MW data center near Sandusky, and has bought land in Conesville, where it has not yet broken ground.

Core Scientific, a bitcoin miner, is converting its mining sites into AI data centers.
