In July 2026 it signed a 15-year lease deal with AMD for 529 megawatts of US AI capacity, which Core Scientific said could bring more than $14 billion in revenue, with AMD's deployments starting in 2027. Under certain conditions AMD can reserve another 1,925 megawatts through December 2028, which would take the partnership to about 2.5 gigawatts of power, and AMD received warrants to buy up to 30 million Core Scientific shares at $23.47 each.

The leased sites are in Pecos and Hunt County, Texas, and Muskogee, Oklahoma, where AMD leased 377 megawatts directly, and in Auburn, Alabama, and Dalton, Georgia, where an unnamed cloud provider leased another 152 megawatts under agreements AMD supports. The deals lift Core Scientific's leased customer capacity to roughly 1.1 gigawatts. Colocation, renting out space and power to other companies, made up 83 percent of its second-quarter revenue, while its own bitcoin mining revenue fell 66 percent.

The largest single conversion is at Pecos, Texas, where Core Scientific said in April 2026 it would turn a 300-megawatt bitcoin mining operation into an AI campus of about 1.5 gigawatts, with roughly a gigawatt available to lease and the first new data hall due in early 2027. It has secured an additional 300 megawatts from the local utility and plans to add on-site power generation it has not yet detailed. The company also plans to sell $3.3 billion in high-yield bonds to help pay for the shift.

Franklin County is one of the country's busiest data center markets. Amazon Web Services has three campuses in Hilliard: on Hayden Run Road, between Cosgray and Leppert roads, and on Scioto Darby Road near Interstate 270. Google runs a data center on the former Hartman farm at 5076 S. High St. in Columbus, and STACK Infrastructure has a 60-megawatt campus on Souder Road in New Albany. Smaller sites include Cologix's COL4 in Columbus and Expedient's data centers in Dublin and Upper Arlington.

The fight in Hilliard is over power. AEP plans a 73-megawatt array of 228 natural gas fuel cells on about six acres to run Amazon's Scioto Darby campus. The city tried to rezone the land, then appealed the state air permit, but state law leaves it little say. On September 15, 2026, Hilliard dropped its appeal. "From the beginning, we knew this would be an uphill battle," Council President Emily Cole said. The city plans to test the air once the fuel cells run.

Southwest of Columbus, towns have paused new projects. Jackson Township trustees voted unanimously on May 12, 2026, for a one-year moratorium on data centers on unincorporated land around Grove City, and Pleasant Township approved one earlier in the year. Grove City's council passed its own pause of up to a year 6-1 on June 1, with a task force and a six-month review. Stream Data Centers has mapped a site of more than 300 acres between Rensch and Beatty roads, crossing both townships, but no application had been filed with Grove City, whose zoning does not allow data centers.

Henrico County closed the by-right path to a data center in June 2025, when the Board of Supervisors voted unanimously to require a public hearing and board approval for every new large data center anywhere in the county, including inside White Oak Technology Park, where nine campuses already operate. QTS is moving ahead there under the county's prior rules, planning to add up to 17 buildings across 1,100 acres in Varina, Richmond BizSense reported.

More than 100 residents filled the Varina Area Library on May 19, 2026 for a nearly three-hour town hall on the QTS expansion, called by Supervisor Tyrone Nelson. Other projects await a hearing under the new rules, including Iron Mountain's proposed 200-megawatt White Oak campus and QTS Richmond 5. DC Blox's proposed 10-megawatt project on Hermitage Road and Wagner Urban Logistics' blocked Darbytown Road data center are also on the county's table, along with operating facilities run by Infotel Systems and, in Glen Allen, Uniti's Cavalier Innsbrook.

In May 2024, before the rules changed, supervisors approved 622 acres on East Williamsburg Road for a data center and advanced-manufacturing project by the developer Hourigan; that approval has not been added as a project here yet. Just north of the county line in Glen Allen, Hanover County rejected Tract's Mountain Road Technology Park on May 28, 2026, closing off one of the two projects Henrico residents nearby had worried about.

France's biggest data center project, Campus IA at Fouju in Seine-et-Marne, about 40 kilometers southeast of Paris, won the prefect's approval on July 29, 2026. Backed by the Emirati fund MGX, Nvidia, Mistral AI and the public bank Bpifrance, it is priced at €50 billion and would reach 1.4 gigawatts of power with eleven data center buildings 20 meters tall on 89 hectares. Its first phase, four data centers and a substation on 38 hectares, was due to start in September 2026, and opponents say they will challenge the approval in court.

Fouju, a village of about 650 people, is split. Mayor Jonathan Wochenmayer says the tax money will pay for sidewalks and a school renovation, and that the site, 2.8 kilometers from the village, is the least disruptive place for it. "We'd like Fouju to stay as it is," retiree Giuliano Del Negro told AFP. The collective Stop IA à Fouju calls the public inquiry botched and points to 613 backup generators and 601 tonnes of cooling gas that could release PFAS "forever chemicals" if it leaked.

North of Paris, the worry is how many data centers are packed together: about thirty have gone up in Seine-Saint-Denis in a decade. At Le Bourget, the new mayor, Mehdi Nezzar, withdrew the permit his predecessor gave Segro for a data center on the former H&M site, and on July 28, 2026, the Montreuil administrative court refused to suspend that withdrawal, leaving the project blocked. "If the project goes ahead, I'm thinking of moving," Adil Champion, who lives less than 200 meters from the site, told Synth Média.

South of Paris, CloudHQ opened the first phase of its campus at Lisses in Essonne in 2025; it plans two buildings of 74.4 megawatts each, and their waste heat is to warm up to 7,000 homes through Corbeil-Essonnes' heating network.

By November 2025 Johor the state had approved 51 projects, with 17 running, 11 under construction and 23 not yet started, w.media reported. Around Kulai and Sedenak Tech Park sit YTL's Green Data Center Park, planned for up to 600 megawatts of power with its first 72 megawatts running, and Vantage's JHB1 campus, which Vantage says will reach more than 300 megawatts across three buildings. In Iskandar Puteri, STACK is building a 220-megawatt campus due to open in late 2026, and AirTrunk plans two more campuses, JHB3 and JHB4, of more than 280 megawatts.

Water is the local fight. In November 2025 the state told developers whose cooling depends on water to wait until mid-2027 for new supply, and stopped approving Tier 1 and Tier 2 data centers, which it says use far more water. That month a sand mining accident cut water to more than half of Johor's 1.7 million residents, sometimes for up to 12 hours. In February 2026 residents of Gelang Patah protested outside a data center construction site because they feared there would not be enough water left for them, The Diplomat reported.

Every new project now goes to a state technical committee that checks its water and power needs. "Even if a data centre achieves a WUE below 1.8, approval still depends on the availability of sufficient water," state official Mohamad Fazli Mohamad Salleh said, referring to the state's water-efficiency limit. Some operators, including Bridge Data Centres, cool with treated sewage water instead of the public supply, and a new treatment plant at Semanggar is being built to add 50 million liters a day for Kulai and Sedenak.

Seven data center projects are proposed or under construction in Spotsylvania County. Amazon Web Services is building its Cosner Tech Campus and its Mattameade/Orrock Tech Campus, which is set for 770 megawatts of power, and has proposed the Summit Crossing and Carter's Store tech campuses. SpotsyTech Campus in Thornburg is approved, and PowerHouse 95 and Gateway Commerce Center are also planned, all in the Fredericksburg and Thornburg areas.

The county has spent 2026 tightening the rules rather than adding projects. On February 25 the Board of Supervisors voted 4-3 to require a special use permit for every data center, ending by-right approval in office, commercial and industrial districts; Chancellor District Supervisor Gerald Childress voted no, warning it could "push away one of the best economic development opportunities in this county." On August 13 the board voted 4-2 to ask Governor Abigail Spanberger to impose a statewide moratorium so the state can study whether to keep permitting the industry, following a call from state Senator Glen Sturtevant. Courtland Supervisor Drew Mullins voted no, telling colleagues "we can be the moratorium" through case-by-case review. On August 26 the board voted 3-2 to cap data centers at 45% of the county's industrially zoned land.

Spotsylvania already bars data centers from cooling equipment with drinking water or their own wells, and requires natural noise buffers; Amazon's Cosner Tech project has separately agreed to a lower noise limit at its property line.

The Netherlands still bars the biggest data centers, those covering at least 10 hectares and drawing 70 megawatts of power or more, from everywhere except two zones: Hollands Kroon in North Holland, where Google and Microsoft run data centers at Middenmeer, and Het Hogeland in Groningen, home to Eemshaven. The ban began as a temporary halt on February 16, 2022, the same year Meta dropped its planned campus at Zeewolde after local opposition. Today the tighter limit is the power grid, which is full around Amsterdam and Schiphol.

On April 29, 2026, a court in Arnhem ruled that grid operator TenneT could keep work paused on a 70-megawatt connection for Goodman's planned data center at Vijfhuizen in Haarlemmermeer, finding the regional grid "genuinely at full capacity." TenneT has told companies near Schiphol the shortage could last until around 2035. Amsterdam stopped new large data centers in June 2025, but earlier approvals still stand: in July 2026 the city issued Equinix a building permit on the Amstel III business park in Zuidoost.

Equinix will build one of the four planned towers at Amstel III for now. At full size the site would need 80 megawatts and use about 779 million kilowatt-hours a year; all Amsterdam households used 869 million in 2024. A city spokesperson said the municipality faces large damage claims if it pulls out.

In Lelystad, Equinix plans a 150-megawatt data center at the Flevokust Haven business park under zoning approved in 2021. Council members were told it would use as much power as 3,000 to 5,000 households; experts consulted by NU.nl put it closer to 200,000. Its three buildings cover at most 7.5 hectares, so the national ban does not apply. North Holland, which had 67 data centers in 2025 and about 20 more seeking permits, is rewriting its plan to allow new ones only inside existing clusters.

Google wants to build a $200 million data center on about 23 hectares on Camino a Lonquén in Cerrillos, a district of Santiago, on the same land where Chile's environmental court stopped its first design in 2024. On June 17, 2026, Google's Chilean subsidiary, Dataluna, asked the Environmental Evaluation Service (SEA) to rule that the redesigned, air-cooled project does not need a full environmental review. Google says it has not yet decided whether to build, and the SEA's answer is still pending.

The neighborhood group MOSACAT and the Latin American Observatory of Environmental Conflicts (OLCA) have asked the SEA to require a full review with public participation, arguing it is essentially the project approved in 2020. That design would have drawn up to 169 liters of water a second from the Santiago Central aquifer. On February 26, 2024, the Second Environmental Court partly annulled the approval, finding too little evidence to rule out serious harm to the aquifer, and Google later gave up the permit.

The new design swaps water cooling for 63 air-cooled condensers and adds 44 backup diesel generators, with 695.9 tonnes of diesel stored on site, below the 1,000-tonne level that has triggered a formal review since January 2026. Building would take 30 months in four phases. MOSACAT's Tania Rodríguez told Down To Earth the group persuaded Google to drop water cooling, but that the change went through without a new environmental assessment.

Elsewhere in greater Santiago, the table below lists Google's and Microsoft's operating sites in Quilicura, Amazon's data center under construction at Padre Hurtado and TECfusions' proposed 100-megawatt campus in Puente Alto.

County Dublin is the second-largest data center market in Europe, with about 1,150 megawatts of power in use by mid-2025, mostly in business parks in west and north Dublin. The latest big approval came in December 2025, when An Coimisiún Pleanála gave Amazon Web Services permission for three more data centers, 73 megawatts in all, on its 65-acre campus at Cruiserath Road in Dublin 15, three years after the plans were filed.

Five parties had appealed Fingal County Council's 2023 approval, including Friends of the Earth and the Fingal One Future Group. The board let it go ahead because the site already has a grid connection and an EirGrid power agreement, on condition that Amazon buys new renewable power at least equal to what the buildings use. Amazon's consultants put the whole Cruiserath campus at 262,535 tonnes of carbon dioxide in 2030, 8.8% of the national cap for the electricity sector.

In Tallaght, where Amazon has run data centers since 2011, waste heat from its buildings on the old Jacob's biscuit factory site on Belgard Road warms council buildings through the Tallaght District Heating Scheme, opened in 2023. The heat link was a condition of permission for the second data center there.

New sites are harder to get. From 2021 EirGrid effectively stopped connecting new data centers around Dublin. The rules that replaced that freeze in December 2025 make each new one bring its own generation or batteries, meet 80% of its yearly use from new Irish renewables, and reject any site where the grid would need major upgrades, a test that bites hardest in Dublin. Environmental groups are challenging the rules in the High Court, with a hearing scheduled for May 2027.

Florida's largest approved data center is in Fort Meade in Polk County, where city commissioners unanimously approved Stonebridge's AI data center on more than 1,300 acres. It cannot move forward until the city gets a new water permit, which the Southwest Florida Water Management District's board must approve at a public meeting. Commissioner Matthew Taylor, who says a recall petition against him is retaliation for backing the project, sued on September 8 to stop the recall; a judge has not yet ruled.

Two other Polk County plans are on hold. Cielo Digital Infrastructure's data center on Marion Road in Haines City, which would use 150,000 gallons of water a day, is stalled because the city has no spare water capacity. In Lakeland, Ryan Companies' Project Swan at 923 Wilkinson Road, which the developer said would draw about 100 megawatts of power at full build-out, led commissioners to vote 4-3 on August 3 for a one-year moratorium on data centers and other users of 50 megawatts or more.

In Palm Beach County, commissioners voted 5-1 on July 15 to reject Project Tango, PBA Holdings' 3.6-million-square-foot data center and warehouse campus at 20125 Southern Boulevard near Loxahatchee, about 900 to 1,200 feet from Saddle View Elementary School. PBA has appealed, which sends the case to a special magistrate, and a 2016 approval still lets it build a 206,000-square-foot data center there. The county stopped taking new data center applications July 9; a final vote on a yearlong moratorium was scheduled for September 24, and no result has been published.

Elsewhere, Deltona Corporation withdrew its plan for an 800-acre industrial park in Holder, in Citrus County, that could have included a data center, on June 23. DeSoto County's one-year moratorium, adopted July 28, does not cover DCIP Group's pending request to rezone more than 800 acres at a former power plant, so that project can still advance. Citrus, Clay, Hernando, Lake, Nassau, Pasco and Sarasota counties have one-year pauses, and Jackson and Walton counties have permanent bans. Escambia County banned large data centers in its unincorporated areas in August.

The state's new law, SB 484, took effect July 1 and lets local governments set stricter rules or refuse a project outright. Manatee County's moratorium is tentatively set for its second commission vote October 6, and Orange County, which contains Orlando, could take up its own in early December.

Sarpy County has five operating data centers: Meta's campus in Springfield, Google's in Papillion, two TierPoint sites in Bellevue and Papillion, and H5 Data Centers in La Vista. Meta's four-million-square-foot Springfield campus is the county's largest and one of the few in the country where a company publishes its own water use.

From 2020 to 2024, Meta's campus withdrew between 26.7 million and 37.5 million gallons of water a year from the local supply, cooling its buildings with a mix of evaporative and closed-loop systems, according to figures Meta self-reports. Google, which built its Papillion site in 2019, reports its Nebraska water use differently, by consumption rather than withdrawal, and does not break the number out by site.

A law passed in the Nebraska Legislature's 2026 session will require the state Department of Water, Energy and Environment to start collecting annual water and energy figures from data centers later this year. Until then, the public figures on any Sarpy County site come only from the companies themselves.

Douglas County has at least 11 data center sites, most already operating, and in July 2026 commissioners rejected a large new one for the second time in seven months. EdgeConneX, filing as East Village Dothan LLC, wanted about 700 acres near Liberty Road rezoned for six buildings and a substation; part of the site lies in the Dog River Basin, the county's main water source. Commissioners voted 4-1 to deny it, following a unanimous no from the Planning and Zoning Commission.

The county's planning manager, Allison Duncan, said unincorporated Douglas County already has about 2.5 million square feet of data center space in eight buildings, including STACK Infrastructure's 160-megawatt Lithia Springs campus, Switch's 150-megawatt Switch Keep, and sites for Google, Aligned Data Centers, DataBank, T5 Data Centers, CoreWeave/Flexential and Microsoft; Digital Realty runs two more in Austell. She warned the county was at risk of overbuilding. "That's what a data center sounds like," said resident Eileen Roberts, playing a recording of industrial whirring at the hearing. "That's 365 days a year, 24/7."

The county has also paused new applications for data centers larger than 50,000 square feet since March 2026, a freeze extended to study what new power lines would cost ratepayers. "New power generation infrastructure ... tends to require 40 to 50 years to pay off," Duncan said.

Lombardy has most of Italy's data centers and its loudest fight over them. On August 4, 2026, the national government declared K2 Strategic Infrastructure Italy's campus of up to about 400 megawatts, worth €5.3 billion, in Zibido San Giacomo and Lacchiarella south of Milan, of strategic national interest, which speeds approval under a special government commissioner. Residents can comment until November 3 on the reopened environmental review for expanding the Noovle data center in Rozzano, and a network of citizens' committees has called a regional demonstration for October 10.

The towns say they were not asked. Zibido's mayor, Sonia Belloli, said she had no answer from the grid operator Terna about a substation planned right beside the site, and no sufficient assurances about its effect on residents. "They talk about billions in investments, but the reality is a devastating impact on our territory," said Zibido councillor Pietro Cataldi, calling the decision "imposed from above." About 200 people marched against data centers in Lacchiarella in July.

Opponents have organized. In September dozens of committees, from Rho and Trezzano sul Naviglio to Travagliato and Magenta, formed the Network of Citizens' Committees Stop Data Center, which wants the health effects of many plants weighed together rather than one at a time. In Travagliato, near Brescia, the province found grounds in August to block a 120-megawatt project's request for a 300-megawatt grid connection, and the developer withdrew its plan from the town. "The mobilization front is growing," said Enrico Duranti of the network.

Lombardy passed Italy's first data center law in June 2026. It steers new sites to disused or contaminated industrial land, bans cooling with drinking or irrigation water, doubles building charges on farmland and triples them in protected parks, and puts the region in charge of projects over 50 megawatts. The Milan area alone had 33 data centers running, 10 under construction and 23 under review, Il Sole 24 Ore reported.

Allegheny County's data center fight is in Springdale, a square-mile borough 18 miles above Pittsburgh. In December 2025 its council voted 5-2 to grant a conditional use permit - a required local approval - to Allegheny DC for a data center on the closed Cheswick power plant site, which abuts homes on three sides. The project's power draw remains unresolved: the plan approved in December 2025 called for 180 megawatts, while later filings for the renamed Dynamo DC project put it as high as 330 megawatts, the figure used here. The county Health Department has not yet ruled on an air permit for the site's backup diesel generators.

None of the council members wanted to vote yes. "I love this town," Jason Overly said before voting for it. "Do I want to see this data center come in? No I don't. But unfortunately we're going to be sued." State law makes approval mandatory once an applicant meets the zoning code, Borough Manager Terry Carcella said, and Springdale had no data center rules of its own when Allegheny DC applied. Duquesne Light's David Fisfis said the utility has no control over generation costs and expects customers to pay an extra $212 million after this summer's power auction.

At a June 2026 open house, the developer's consultants said they had added mufflers and acoustic barriers, and that the generators would need to pass a county air-permit review before construction. "We do not need a data center," said retired therapist Carole Brennan. "Our children are much more important." Protesters organized by the Breathe Project are asking the Health Department to require that permit, and to follow extra review rules for state-designated environmental justice areas, before construction can proceed.

Other data centers already operate in the county, including Expedient's two Pittsburgh sites, Ascent Data and Lumen in Pittsburgh, and the Ardent Data Center in McKees Rocks. On August 25, 2026, county council members Dan Grzybek and Bethany Hallam introduced a bill to ban data centers on the county's own land; it has nearly enough co-sponsors to pass and remains in committee.

Three big campuses are going up in Wisconsin: Microsoft's $20 billion complex at Mount Pleasant in Racine County, which began opening this summer; Lighthouse, the $15 billion Vantage, Oracle and OpenAI campus at Port Washington in Ozaukee County; and Meta's $1 billion data center at Beaver Dam in Dodge County. A draft state report says the three account for nearly three-quarters of an expected 40% rise in Wisconsin's peak electricity demand by 2032.

In Port Washington, developers spent at least $125 million on 1,500 acres or more, often paying far above assessed value. "On paper it looked OK, until you go to replace what you had," said Ryan Nowak, who sold 65 acres and now lives on 1.5. In August state regulators sent American Transmission Company back to the start of its application for the more than $1.3 billion in lines and substations needed to power the campus; ATC has not said when it will refile.

At least 24 Wisconsin communities have adopted moratoriums, usually for a year, among them Madison, Superior, Middleton and Dane, Door, Grant, Manitowoc, Dodge and Jefferson counties. In Grant County, where developers proposed a $1 billion-plus data center, the town of Cassville rejected the zoning it needed. In Menomonie, a stalled plan by Balloonist LLC on more than 300 acres is on hold while the city writes rules. The Public Service Commission still has to rule on the data center power rates proposed by Alliant Energy for Beaver Dam and We Energies for Mount Pleasant and Port Washington.

Saline Township's board voted to deny the rezoning for a large Oracle-and-OpenAI data center campus; the developer, Related Digital, and the landowners sued, arguing the refusal was illegal exclusionary zoning, and the township settled by consent judgment filed October 15, 2025, letting the roughly $7 billion project proceed. A trustee called the settlement the lesser of two evils. The project, reported at both 1,383 and 1,400 megawatts in different accounts, is now under construction.

In exchange, the judgment bars the operator from expanding the site, sets a noise limit, bans solar farms there, and requires closed-loop rather than water-intensive cooling. The developer is paying $2 million to the township for farmland preservation and $2 million into a community fund, with $7 million more to the Saline Area Fire Department. Its local tax break came in nine times smaller than requested. A resident's Open Meetings Act challenge to the deal, and a request to slow construction, were both rejected by a judge in February 2026.

Elsewhere in the county, Augusta Township voters overturned a rezoning for Thor Equities' proposed $1 billion data center by about 90% in an August 2026 ballot vote, blocking it. In Ypsilanti, the University of Michigan and Los Alamos National Laboratory are still proposing a $1.2 billion data center that Los Alamos has confirmed would support nuclear weapons research, drawing protests over the site.

Amazon Web Services is building a large data center off Alcovy Road near Highway 142 in Covington, and Meta has run a data center campus at Stanton Springs since breaking ground in 2018. A third campus, the Gregory Road Data Center, would put up to 1.41 million square feet of buildings on about 213 acres just south of Lake Varner, the county's drinking water reservoir and needs Covington to annex the land first. Newton County's pause on new data center applications runs until October 7, 2026.

Amazon is paying for a water reuse plant, estimated at about $180 million, that the city will own, and will make more than $300 million in payments in place of property taxes through 2041, plus about $215 million in electricity franchise fees to Covington. In July 2026 the city halted work at the Amazon site after runoff from a detention pond "discharged turbid water above the allowed limits"; the order was later lifted with conditions.

On Hazelbrand Road in Covington, Serverfarm is building a data center powered by VoltaGrid's 90-megawatt gas-fired plant next door. State environmental regulators cited both companies on July 2, 2026, for starting construction before they had air permits, and ordered VoltaGrid to stop building its engines. "Covington and Newton County communities deserve transparency, accountability, and a voice," said Maurice Carter of Sustainable Newton.

County rules allow data centers only in the Stanton Springs area, so developers have asked cities to annex land instead; Covington refused one such request, a 1,500-acre site on Elks Club Road, in January. Covington paused data center requests on January 20 and lifted the pause on August 31, after adopting rules that allow the largest data centers only in heavy industrial zones with a special permit and a buffer of at least 250 feet from homes. The county's own pause, set on February 17 and extended twice, ends October 7 unless commissioners extend it again.

South Africa's data centers are concentrated around Johannesburg, where Teraco's Isando campus has 70 megawatts of power for computers and its Bredell campus 63, and Cape Town is next. On July 14, 2026, Cape Town's Municipal Planning Tribunal approved Equinix's plan for two data centers on the old King David golf course next to Cape Town International Airport, with a peak demand of up to 160 megawatts. The objectors' lawyers at the Legal Resources Centre said they were considering an appeal.

The Housing Assembly and the London group Foxglove objected that the rezoning rested on a 24-page letter "that says nothing about water, nothing about emissions," in a city that nearly ran out of water in 2018. Equinix says the buildings will use dry, air-based cooling. Four large projects planned in Cape Town, including a 360-megawatt campus announced by the Cavaleros Group, would together need 580 megawatts, just over a third of the city's current peak demand.

In September 2026 civil rights groups called for a halt to new data centers until their use of water, land and electricity has been investigated. The South African Human Rights Commission has received more than 250 submissions in its own inquiry. Eskom, the state power company, came through the winter with a surplus, and campaigners fear that power will be sold to data centers.

In Durban, eThekwini's council agreed in February 2026 to explore an AI data center in the south of the city with a Korean consortium; the city says only the exploratory agreement was approved, not a project. Teraco's existing Durban data center, DB1, has 2.2 megawatts.

The UAE's biggest data center project is the UAE-US AI Campus in Abu Dhabi, a 10-square-mile site that G42's Khazna Data Centers plans to grow to about 5 gigawatts of power. Its first piece is Stargate UAE, a 1-gigawatt cluster built with OpenAI, Oracle, Nvidia, Cisco and SoftBank. Its first 200 megawatts were due in the third quarter of 2026; in August Khazna said two 100-megawatt buildings were enclosed with equipment going in and that it was on track to hand over capacity to customers this year.

Khazna, which controls most of the country's data center capacity, says it runs about 300 megawatts in the UAE with almost 370 more under construction or commissioning. That includes a 100-megawatt campus in Ajman, 20 halls of 5 megawatts each, and 200 megawatts for Microsoft due before the end of 2026. In Dubai, the telecom company du signed a $544.54 million deal with Microsoft in 2025 for a new large data center.

The 2026 war with Iran reached the industry here. Amazon said two of its UAE data centers were struck by drones in March, and in September it said some customer data held only in the damaged facilities could not be recovered. Power is the other pressure: Wood Mackenzie estimates UAE data centers used 3 terawatt-hours in 2025, about 2% of national demand, and will use more than 6 by 2030. Khazna's commercial chief, Greg Jasmin, said the campus depends as much on new power generation and transmission as on the buildings.

Marion County has stopped permitting new data centers until December 31, 2027. The Indianapolis City-County Council voted 23-1 on August 10, 2026 to approve the pause, and the Metropolitan Development Commission gave it final approval, 6-0, on August 19. Until then the county's zoning code did not define a data center; the council added one from the floor covering any facility built primarily to store, manage, process or transmit digital data, including AI training and cloud computing.

The pause is meant to produce permanent rules, not just delay. City staff are to convene a committee on campus size, building height, noise levels and environmental impact before the moratorium ends. It does not cover projects already approved: Sabey's 250-megawatt campus in Decatur Township, DC Blox's Thunderbird Commerce Center in Warren Township and Metrobloks' Brightwood project in Martindale-Brightwood are all exempt, so the residents who fought hardest against those three got a pause that does not touch them.

The county also has two smaller data centers already running, Lifeline Data Center and US Signal Data Center, both in Indianapolis. American Tower has suspended its 4-megawatt Edge Data Center project, and Google withdrew its Franklin Township proposal. Equinix lists a data hub in Indianapolis on its own materials, but the company's own current world map of its markets does not include Indianapolis, so its size and status here are unclear.

The biggest data center in Jackson County is Nebius's campus on nearly 400 acres near Missouri Highway 78 and Little Blue Parkway in eastern Independence. It broke ground in May and will need at least 800 megawatts of power, which a reopened Blue Valley power plant is to supply. Patmos is also planning a data center in a warehouse at 2500 Little Blue Parkway, with construction priced at about $107 million. Neither project is covered by the 180-day pause on new data center applications that Independence adopted on July 6.

The Independence City Council approved a 90% tax break for Nebius over 20 years, worth $6.26 billion, on a 5-2 vote in March. Residents tried to force a public vote on it, but a judge sided with the city. Voters then elected Kevin King mayor with 60% of the vote. On September 1 they recalled council member John Perkins, who had backed the tax break. "Who's going to want to live next to that?" asked Dawn Hahnfeld, who lives nearby.

In Kansas City, the Plan Commission voted 6-0 in August to deny Revitalization Unlimited's 384-foot data center on top of a historic building in the Quality Hill neighborhood. Jackson County has paused data center land use applications for 180 days from June 22 while it writes rules on safety and distance from homes. The county's pause ends December 19 unless it is extended.

Hanover County has turned down its two biggest data center proposals. On May 28, 2026, the Board of Supervisors voted 4-3 against rezoning nearly 430 acres in western Hanover for Tract's 900-megawatt Mountain Road Technology Park, overriding its own planning commission, which had recommended approval 6-1 six weeks earlier. Supervisors Faye Prichard, Danielle Floyd, Sean Davis and Jeff Stoneman voted to deny; Sue Dibble, F. Michael Herzberg and Ryan Hudson voted to approve.

Water use decided it. The project could have used up to 2 million gallons a day, and Hanover buys its drinking water from the City of Richmond rather than producing its own. "I don't know if it goes far enough to meet the needs," Stoneman said of Tract's offer to help pay for a new pump station and water tank.

It was the second Hanover data center to fail this year. HHHunt withdrew its 900-megawatt, 400-acre Hunting Hawk campus near Wyndham on February 3, 2026, days before a scheduled vote, after planners recommended denial. A separate Tract proposal in Ashland, the roughly 1,200-acre Hickory Hill Road campus approved in 2024, is moving ahead and is not the same project as Mountain Road. A fourth proposal, Tract's Iron Horse, was deferred on June 19, 2026 and has not returned to the board since.

Edged is building a 200-megawatt data center campus, known as Project Lola, at College Road and East Kanesville Boulevard in Council Bluffs. The first of its two buildings was topped out in June 2026 and the second was due to be in September. Google has run a data center campus in the city for years, and in June 2026 the City Council voted 5-0 against a one-year pause on new data centers.

Mayor Jill Shudak asked for the pause so the city could write data center rules and check its water and sewer capacity. "We're running very high at capacity for both water and sewer," she said. Public Works Director Matt Cox said a single large project can use as much wastewater capacity as about 4,000 homes, and a new treatment plant could cost $200 million to $300 million. Councilman Douglas Rew said a pause would make the city look "closed off" to developers.

Council members said a wastewater plan was the better next step and that new zoning rules could be written without a moratorium. Google said its Council Bluffs campus used 1.3 billion gallons of water in 2025, more than any of its other data center sites. At the June hearing, county resident Roger Williams said vibrations from soil work at a data center construction site had damaged his home.

Carroll County has four data center projects on record. Atlas Development's Atlas Villa Rica project has been approved, and Atlas has a second Villa Rica filing, the Avemore GA LLC Data Center, still listed as proposed. FOGO Solutions already operates FOGO Carrollton, and Atlas withdrew a third project, called Project Bus, in Temple.

Commissioners voted 7-0 on March 3, 2026 for a 100-day moratorium on permits for data centers and battery storage systems in unincorporated Carroll County, after months of residents speaking against data center development at commission meetings. On June 3 they extended it 7-0 for another 100 days, which would have run out around September 11, 2026; whether commissioners have voted since then to extend it again is not confirmed in the local reporting we could verify.

The pause covers only unincorporated Carroll County, not its cities, the same gap developers elsewhere in Georgia have used by seeking annexation into a town. A public petition opposing the Villa Rica projects has run alongside the commission meetings, and pressure from that fight is what turned into the countywide moratorium.

Selangor approved 39 data center projects between 2021 and 2025, and several large ones are being built now. Google said in August 2026 that its $2 billion data center at Elmina Business Park should open within nine months, and Vantage is building its KUL2 campus in Cyberjaya, which it says will offer 436 megawatts of power when complete. On September 8, 2026, Menteri Besar Amirudin Shari said no data center will be approved without guaranteed water and electricity.

Residents in Kota Damansara, Petaling Jaya, stopped one plan this summer. A proposed three-story data center on Jalan Rimba Riang 9/6 in Section 9 drew about 290 formal objections, including one from a coalition of more than 500 households worried about noise, round-the-clock operation, heat and traffic. The developer's consultant withdrew the application on July 28, 2026, to rethink the site, the city council said. "Thank you to all KD people," assemblyman Muhammad Izuan Ahmad Kasim posted.

Water is the main worry. Any project expected to use more than two million liters a day must now file a detailed water study, and developers must lay their own supply pipes and store three days of water on site. The state says Air Selangor has spare capacity and that the Rasau scheme will add 350 million liters a day, rising to 700 million when its first phase is finished.

Eagle Rock Partners is a Charlotte-based development firm whose data center campuses have met resistance in three states. On Aug. 12, 2026 it abandoned Meridian Technology Park, a planned $6 billion, 1,000-megawatt campus on farmland southwest of Taylorville in Christian County, Illinois; the county board president said the company feared its planned power supplier, the long-delayed Lincoln Land Energy Center gas plant, may never be built.

About 400 people, most of them opposed, had turned out at a June 16 county board meeting, and a petition for an immediate 18-month moratorium on data centers in Christian County gathered just short of 700 signatures.

In Georgia, Eagle Rock Partners and Thomas & Hutton Engineering withdrew their application to rezone more than 600 acres in Jones County for the Crooked Creek Technology Park in October 2025, before its planning and zoning hearing and amid organized opposition. Jones County commissioners then created a new zone where data centers are a conditional use, and residents sued, saying the process denied them proper notice. "We're dead in the water," the development authority's attorney, Kevin Brown, said of the industrial park while the lawsuit is pending.

In neighboring Twiggs County, commissioners voted on Sept. 18, 2025 to rezone 291.5 acres for an Eagle Rock Partners data center, after weeks of debate about water, energy and the local black bear population. The site near Dry Branch is owned by an affiliate of the timber company Weyerhaeuser, and the project was reported at $5 billion.

In South Carolina, Eagle Rock Partners proposes a $6 billion, nine-building, 860-acre campus on timberland near Walterboro in Colleton County, which would be the state's first gigawatt data center. At a packed three-hour meeting in December 2025 only founding partner Ken Loeber spoke in favor, while residents, environmental groups and a state senator objected to its closeness to the ACE Basin estuary and its possible draw on the Ashepoo River and groundwater.

"The most significant conservation achievement in the state of South Carolina, I'd dare say on the entire East Coast, is the protection of the ACE Basin," state Sen. Chip Campsen told the county zoning board.

Compass Datacenters is expanding in Red Oak, Texas, over organized opposition. In May 2026 the city council voted 4-1, late at night, to rezone about 830 acres of farmland into a planned "high tech industrial park" for what would be the city's sixth Compass campus. Residents packed city hall, citing noise, traffic and how close the site would sit to homes. "We're supposed to look out for the welfare of our people," said organizer Elda Jazmin Villegas. Her group, now renamed Save Our Red Oak, is raising money through car shows for a legal challenge.

In June 2026, Ellis County accepted a $15 million donation from Compass for a new county animal shelter, and Compass gave Texas State Technical College $12.6 million for a data center training building. Some residents questioned the gifts' timing. "I hate to think that we're going to be obligated to Compass," said Waxahachie resident Susie Hall; County Judge John Wray said the donations carry no obligations. A tax abatement for Compass's 890-acre property was withdrawn before the June 23 commissioners meeting, which founder and chief executive Chris Crosby attributed to public "noise."

In Mississippi, Compass is building a $10 billion hyperscale complex in Lauderdale County, near Meridian. The Center for Economic Accountability, a Michigan nonprofit, named it the worst economic development deal of 2025. "There's a lot of bad, dumb data center deals out there, and Mississippi became pretty clearly a standout," said the center's president, John Mozena.

Nordland has one of Europe's largest AI data centers under construction and more planned. In Narvik, the British company Nscale is building a campus for Microsoft and its customer OpenAI; its first phase will use about 230 megawatts of power, and contractors are already preparing a second, bigger phase. Nscale also runs a data center at Glomfjord, and the Hemnes municipal council approved the zoning for Nscale's planned 250-megawatt data center at Korgen on June 10, 2026; that decision can be appealed within three weeks of notice.

The Narvik project began as Stargate Norway, meant to be OpenAI's first European site, but in April 2026 Nscale dropped the Stargate name and Microsoft took OpenAI's place, TIME reported. About 350 workers were on site in March, with at least 1,500 expected. Narvik's municipal administrator, Lars Norman Andersen, supports the project and expects 200 jobs. "It's obviously beneficial that we utilize the green electricity here, instead of sending it to London or Stockholm," said site manager Torkjell Lund, who grew up in Narvik.

Not everyone agrees. Lars Haltbrekken, a left-wing member of parliament, warns that a wave of data centers could push up power prices and use up electricity Norway needs. In Mo i Rana, T1 Energy has been assigned 50 megawatts of grid power by Statnett to turn a former battery factory into a data center.

Fayetteville has one data center campus, and it has decided that is enough. QTS is building what Atlanta News First called Georgia's largest data center on about 600 acres along Highway 54 West between Veterans Parkway and Tyrone Road, 22 miles south of downtown Atlanta: up to 13 buildings and about 6.2 million square feet, with construction expected to run until about 2030. QTS estimates the campus will generate $150 million to $200 million a year in real property tax and about $170 million in sales tax, figures the city repeats on its own website. On March 5, 2026 the City Council adopted Ordinance 26-0-12, which makes new data centers a prohibited use in every zoning district in the city.

The ban's first casualty was a second project. Crow Holdings Development and CHI/Acquisitions wanted a single two-story, 300,000-square-foot data center and a substation on a 37.4-acre parcel on Highway 85 North, just past the Fayette Pavilion shopping center. The land was already zoned for it, so the developer's only obstacle was the Planning and Zoning Commission, which rejected the site plan on January 27. The developer appealed to the council, then withdrew the appeal on March 18, the day before the hearing. "I believe the people have spoken and CHI listened," Councilman Emmett Spurlock told The Citizen, crediting a town hall the council had held. No capacity was ever disclosed, and what will now be built on the site is not known.

The fight that shaped both decisions was over QTS's water. In May 2025, after a neighbor near the Annelise Park subdivision complained of low water pressure, the county water director, Vanessa Tigert, wrote to QTS that a meter had been installed "without the knowledge or inspection" of county staff, and the county billed the company about $147,000. When the letter surfaced through a records request in 2026, the county walked it back: "Our letter was unclear." County Administrator Steve Rapson told The Citizen that staff had inspected the meter but believed it was being read electronically during a switch to smart meters, and that it was not. "It's not like they put a meter in, threw a camel net over it, and we didn't know," he said. QTS paid, and says it has stayed within its permitted estimates. Atlanta News First's analysis of billing records found the county had billed QTS for 109 million gallons across 13 water lines since February 2024, which QTS says went on concrete, dust control and site preparation.

The county and QTS say the construction demand will fall away. QTS says each finished building will use about as much water as four American households, because its closed-loop cooling recirculates the same water, and the county says QTS uses less than 1 percent of its daily production. Neighbors are unconvinced. "If my daughter down here tapped into that big pipeline down the road without putting a meter on it, she'd be in jail," Willard Neal, 87, who lives near the site, told Atlanta News First. "A data center is not going to jail." He called living beside it "terrible," citing tree clearing, construction and a constant hum. A few miles away in Tyrone, the county's other approved project, Microsoft's Project Rita Campus, is moving ahead at 96 megawatts of power, the only other capacity figure reported in the county.
The Memphis fight is not about whether a data center should be built. It is about whether the gas turbines powering it needed a permit, and it has been going on for two years.

The Greater Memphis Chamber announced in June 2024 that xAI would build a supercomputer in Memphis. Shortly after, the company began installing methane gas turbines at the site that became Colossus 1, without a permit. xAI applied for a permit for 15 turbines in January 2025, but aerial photos that April found 35 running. After a 60-day notice of intent to sue filed on behalf of the NAACP, xAI removed the unpermitted turbines in June 2025; the health department approved a 15-turbine permit that July anyway. The EPA closed the loophole in January 2026, ruling that turbines need permits even when called temporary or portable. The NAACP, represented by SELC and Earthjustice, sued xAI under the Clean Air Act in April 2026 and sought an injunction to shut the turbines down in May.

Colossus 1 runs at 340 megawatts and Colossus 2, which is expanding, at 946 megawatts; Colossus 2 sits at Tulane Road in Whitehaven, a historic Black neighborhood in southwest Memphis. In September 2026 the council discussed spending nearly $3.3 million in tax revenue from the xAI site on home repairs, blight cleanup and air-quality monitoring within five miles of the property.

The council is also considering a one-year pause on new data center rezoning, site plans and building permits, sponsored by council chair Jana Swearengen-Washington, Yolanda Cooper-Sutton and former chair J.B. Smiley. A committee advanced it August 18, 2026. The full council is scheduled to vote on it October 6, 2026.

Millard County, a desert county of about 13,400 people in central Utah, has approved two of the largest data center campuses ever proposed, and its commissioners say they are glad to have them. The first is Creekstone Energy's campus outside Delta, on nearly 1,200 acres rezoned from agricultural to heavy industrial for a 20 million square foot campus called the Delta Gigasite. Creekstone, led by Ray Conley, says it will manage up to 10 gigawatts there over the coming decade: 1.8 gigawatts from the Intermountain Power Project next door, 6 gigawatts of solar and 2 of natural gas.

In April 2026 the state awarded the $17 billion project a tax reduction tied to 106 jobs, and Creekstone expects its first computers online by late 2027. BluSky AI has agreed to use 25 acres and up to 50 megawatts of the site's power for modular AI computing, one of the Gigasite's first named tenants.

The second is Joule Capital Partners' campus on about 4,000 acres of the Triple C Farms, rezoned to heavy industrial in August 2025. Joule partner Mark McDougal is part owner of the farm: "This project is actually on the farm that my family and I have been farming for the last two decades," he told the commission.

With Caterpillar and Wheeler Machinery, Joule plans more than 4 gigawatts of on-site gas generation with battery storage, able to run apart from the regional grid. Joule broke ground in November 2025 and expects to start providing power in 2026; the state called it central to Gov. Spencer Cox's Operation Gigawatt.

The county's argument is that these projects bring money without people. "The data centers are probably the best way for us to get development, rather than a business that brings 500 people [for whom] we will have to build houses, schools and everything else," Commissioner Bill Wright told Utah Business. Commissioner Vicki Lyman said the campuses would generate their own power rather than draw on the local grid. Both said the county gave neither developer special incentives.

Residents' worry is water, in one of Utah's driest regions. In Delta, Mack Barnhardt, who spent 44 years in water filtration, told Fox 13 in September 2026 that "losing the water, I think it's our number one concern." Creekstone's answer is a University of Utah research project to capture water from burning natural gas, which it estimates could produce about 4,000 acre-feet a year from 2 gigawatts of gas generation. State Sen. Nate Blouin, D-Salt Lake City, said the developers' original pitch to lawmakers in 2024 "sounded very snake oily."

Neither developer has disclosed a total water figure, a tenant or, for Joule, a cost. What comes next is Joule's first power and computing capacity, due in 2026, and the University of Utah's verdict on Creekstone's water-capture plan.

Pittsylvania County has said both things within a year. In April 2025 its Board of Supervisors voted 6-1 to reject Balico's proposal for data centers and a natural gas power plant, after residents organized as the Coalition for the Protection of Pittsylvania County with help from the Southern Environmental Law Center. Balico's plan had shrunk from an original 2,200 acres, 84 buildings and a 3,500-megawatt gas plant down to 750 acres and 12 data center buildings before the vote.

In May 2026 county and city leaders approved a different one: Stack Infrastructure's AI data center campus at the Southern Virginia Megasite at Berry Hill, described by officials as $100 billion of investment over thirty years, 2,500 permanent jobs and an average wage of around $80,000. "Today is very historic because of the amount of revenue and the investment we are looking at," said Vic Ingram, chair of the Regional Industrial Facilities Authority board.

Some residents near the megasite were not convinced. Erin Hall, who said she lives four miles away, questioned the water and power plans: "They say that they've got the water and power under control, the wells, but what happens if it goes wrong?" She also said the project's public meetings had drawn little public awareness. Ingram said the meetings were well advertised and that he did not know what more the county could do.

The two decisions differed mainly on where the power would come from: Balico proposed building its own gas plant on farmland near homes, while Berry Hill is a state-designated megasite already zoned and serviced for heavy industry.

Port Washington held the first anti-data-center referendum in the United States and passed it with about 66 percent of the vote on April 7, 2026. The measure does not ban anything; it requires voter approval before the city creates any tax incremental financing district worth more than $10 million, the usual way these projects get financed. It followed anger that the city had approved a district for Vantage's Lighthouse campus, a $15 billion project on 647 acres now under construction, without a public vote.

A grassroots group called Great Lakes Neighbors United gathered a thousand signatures to put the measure on the ballot. It had no effect on Lighthouse, which was already approved and being built; it changes every deal after it, since an incentive now has to survive an election rather than a council vote. The Badger Institute has argued that putting incentives to referendum could stall development statewide, but the group that led the campaign calls the result a win for public participation rather than a defeat for the data center.

Chester County's clearest data center fight is over the Pennhurst Data Center, proposed by Pennhurst Holdings LLC on land in East Vincent Township. The company is now seeking a conditional-use permit after township supervisors declined to vote on a stricter data center ordinance; its attorney, Matt McHugh, says the coming hearings will address residents' concerns about water and electricity use. Elsewhere in the county, Sentinel Data Centers is building a data center in East Whiteland Township, Constellation Energy withdrew a proposed Pottstown data center, and Comcast already runs one in West Chester.

Resident Steve Hacker's well in East Vincent Township ran dry for 39 days in October 2024, and he blames the coming data center for what he expects next. "They want to pull millions of gallons of water out. I don't see how that can work," he said. "Who is responsible if all the wells in my town dry out?" He wants a moratorium so officials can slow down, and township supervisors have so far stayed publicly neutral: "We have to keep an open mind," said Supervisor Craig A. Damon II.

State Sen. Katie Muth, whose district includes the site, plans to introduce a bill for a two-year statewide moratorium and wants developers to have a plan for keeping any battery fire from spreading to a nearby nuclear plant. Gov. Josh Shapiro has instead championed the industry, pointing to a planned $20 billion Amazon Web Services investment in eastern Pennsylvania announced in October 2025. The next step in East Vincent is the township's conditional-use hearings on the Pennhurst project.

Skybox Datacenters and Prologis are marketing a future data center campus at Atlantic Station, the former NTT site at 2300 West Plano Parkway. Skybox's plan offers build-to-suit construction and an on-site substation expandable to 100 megawatts of power; the 100-megawatt figure describes a proposed ceiling, not a running data center. The site covers about 64 acres.

Plano also has STACK Infrastructure's DFW01 campus, which advertises 80 megawatts across three buildings, and Aligned's DFW-01 and DFW-02 facilities at 2800 Summit Avenue. CoreWeave announced in July 2023 that it would invest $1.6 billion in a data center at 1000 Coit Road. In Allen, CyrusOne lists 77 megawatts of capacity across its DFW3 and DFW4 facilities, with additional land reserved for future development.

Residents in Plano have asked the City Council for stronger rules before further data center growth. Kyle McGinn urged a moratorium or a separate zoning category as the city rewrites its development code, while Shirley Lawson said residents were ready to organize around the 2027 council elections. In Princeton, the City Council agreed on June 23 to consider zoning restrictions on data centers.

King George County has approved three data center projects and is now fighting one of them in court. The largest, Oasis Digital Properties' Dahlgren West campus near the Navy base at Dahlgren, was approved unanimously in August 2025 for up to 1.2 gigawatts across ten buildings. The second, Green Energy Ventures' 300-acre campus at Kings Highway and Bloomsbury Road, was approved 3-2 in February 2026. The third, Amazon's 869-acre Birchwood campus, was approved by an earlier board in 2023, but the current board voted in early 2024 to rescind the county's agreement with Amazon; local news reported the board was "ready to go to war" with the company. The dispute is now in circuit court, with a trial set for September 2026; no result has been published.

Residents only learned the scale of what had been approved at a June 3, 2026 public-comment session that turned into an unplanned town hall. "This should've happened last year," said Supervisor Ken Stroud. Dahlgren West neighbor Briana Morgan told the board: "We bought our forever home. I've got little kids and I don't want a data center in my backyard." County Administrator Matthew Smolnik told residents the legislative process was already over: "The board of supervisors...are elected by the public...the legislative process is already over. Everything, from here on out, is administrative."

The board did answer some practical questions. Dahlgren West will use treated wastewater, not drinking water, to cool its equipment, and Northern Neck Electric Cooperative is charging the developer the full cost of connecting new power lines. When the first building permit is issued, the developer must pay King George $5 million for schools and county buildings. Virginia has no statewide rule on data centers, leaving decisions like these to counties.

Milam County, between Austin and Waco, has become a place where bitcoin mines are turning into AI data centers. Most of that is happening on the land of Alcoa's old aluminum works at Rockdale, a site of some 33,000 acres where smelting ended in 2008 and the plant closed completely in 2017; buyers point to the large power connections and substations already serving the site. Separately, OpenAI's Stargate campus, built by SoftBank's SB Energy, is going up near Burlington.

Riot Platforms is the biggest operator in Rockdale. It built a seven-building bitcoin mine there between 2020 and 2023, described as the largest crypto mining facility in North America, and in January 2026 bought the 200 acres it occupies for $96 million, paid for by selling about 1,080 bitcoin. It signed a ten-year lease with chip designer AMD for 25 megawatts of computing capacity, delivered in phases from January to May 2026, with room to grow to 200 megawatts, and says it intends to convert the site's full 700 megawatts to data center tenants.

Bitdeer, a bitcoin miner that also sells AI computing, already runs a data center at Rockdale and in September 2026 paid $100 million for 200 more acres of the former Alcoa land next to it. Bitdeer says it has access to 563 megawatts of interconnected grid capacity across the two sites, with potential to expand to 742 megawatts. A state filing registered April 15, 2026 for the Stargate campus's first phase, on County Road 133 in Burlington, describes a 548,950-square-foot data center; construction began in October 2025 and is due to finish in October 2026. Both companies' plans depend on the grid granting more power in the coming years; Data Center Dynamics reported that Texas is under a pause on new data center connection approvals while Governor Greg Abbott orders an audit of the queue.

Ontario has two local pauses on new data centers and a provincial rulebook on the way. Mississauga's council voted unanimously on September 16, 2026 to freeze data centers drawing more than 10 megawatts of power for one year, following Oakville, which passed the province's first moratorium in August. The province's draft Data Centre Playbook closed for comment on September 12; the final version is expected this fall.

Mississauga's vote leaves in limbo a 40-megawatt Prologis project in Meadowvale Business Park, just south of Highway 401 and about a kilometer from the nearest homes. Residents raised its energy use, backup generators and floodplain location. "We've heard your voice loud and clear," said Councilor Martin Reid, who sponsored the pause; he called the provincial playbook encouraging but toothless: "There's no recourse." Prologis said it was disappointed and considering its next steps. Hamilton and Burlington ordered planning studies instead of pauses.

Premier Doug Ford, who has criticized moratoriums, says new data centers will pay all their own power costs and a higher rate than other big industrial users, and must show local benefits and meet water and noise standards. Under a 2025 law, the province now decides which large projects get a grid connection; applications could top 10,000 megawatts, about 40% of Ontario's recent peak demand. In Armour Township, Almaguin Data dropped a proposed AI data center in 2026 after a petition with more than 1,000 signatures.

Around Toronto, STACK runs a campus in Scarborough planned for 56 megawatts, CoreWeave runs an AI data center, due to open in August 2025, in a former BlackBerry building in Cambridge, and Microsoft has been preparing a site in Markham since May 2024, with building construction expected to begin in late 2026.

Denmark's power grid is full, and data centers are being pushed to the back of the line. On March 2, 2026, the state grid operator Energinet stopped signing new large connections after requests reached 60 gigawatts, against national peak demand of just over 7 gigawatts. Emergency legislation introduced on August 20 would give households, small businesses and green-energy projects first call on the grid and put data centers last. Parliament is reviewing it, and the rules are meant to apply when grid requests are next assessed this autumn.

The biggest new plan is Data Center Kassø, on 105 hectares of farmland at Kassøvej 26, about 15 kilometers west of Aabenraa and 2 kilometers from the village of Hjordkær. The applicant, Dapsi International ApS, plans four large buildings over about six years, with up to 185 backup diesel generators and about 400 staff. Aabenraa municipality set the scope of its environmental review on April 27, 2026; an environmental report, a draft permit and a public hearing come next.

Google bought land beside the Kassø substation, where the Danish and German grids meet, in 2017. Denmark's operating data centers include Google's in Fredericia, Meta's in Odense, Apple's in Viborg and Microsoft's around Køge. Climate and Energy Minister Samira Nawa has blamed "foreign datacentres," especially those of "American tech giants," for the strain on the grid.

Batam, the island across the strait from Singapore, is where Indonesia's data center boom is landing, with at least 16 new data centers in various stages there, The Jakarta Post reported in August 2026. The biggest is DayOne's campus at Kabil Industrial Tech Park, which has a deal with the utility PLN Batam for 450 megawatts of power, delivered in phases through 2026 and 2027. DayOne already runs a data center at Nongsa Digital Park.

Water is the local fight. Batam's six reservoirs produce 3,487 liters a second, while large data centers need about 18.93 million liters a day, as much as 10,000 to 50,000 residents use. "The situation of water congestion in Batam is currently like a lottery, it's just a matter of waiting for which housing won't receive water today," said Uba Ingan Sigalingging of the group Gerakan Bersama Rakyat. In December 2024, residents of the Teluk Mata Ikan fishing village protested outside Nongsa Digital Park that its water kept flowing while theirs did not.

Suyono Saputra of Batam International University says the city should put "utility first, investment follows," warning that a supply crisis could hit residents hard if infrastructure lags. The long-term fix, turning seawater into drinking water, needs money and time. Most of Indonesia's other data centers listed below, including AWS and NTT, are east of Jakarta around Cikarang, Cibitung and Karawang.

Nigeria's data centers are clustered in Lagos, and the biggest new one has just opened. Kasi Cloud, backed by the Nigeria Sovereign Investment Authority, commissioned LOS1 in the Maiyegun area of Lekki in May 2026, the first building on a $250 million campus designed to reach about 100 megawatts of power; the first phase was expected to bring about 5.5 megawatts online. Airtel's Nxtra is building a 38-megawatt campus at Eko Atlantic, and Open Access Data Centres is building a 24-megawatt site in Lekki.

Power is the local problem. Nigeria's national grid has never carried more than about 6 gigawatts for 230 million people and is available about 41% of the time, so most data centers run largely on diesel generators. Diesel power costs roughly 40 to 50 cents a kilowatt-hour, against 5 to 10 cents on the grid in South Africa or Kenya. Kasi says its campus will run on gas, solar and batteries.

Smaller projects are also underway. Equinix's $22 million LG3 at 43 Saka Tinubu on Victoria Island was due to open in the first quarter of 2026, as the first step in a $100 million plan for Africa. MTN opened the first phase of a 4.5-megawatt data center in Ikeja in July 2025, with a second phase for AI computing due in the second half of 2026.

Demand is being pushed by law. The National Digital Cloud Policy, released on August 17, 2026, requires national security and defense data to be hosted only on infrastructure in Nigeria, and financial, health, biometric and identity data to be stored in the country. Federal agencies must build new systems for the cloud unless the technology agency NITDA grants a time-limited exemption.

Los Angeles County has banned new large AI data centers in its unincorporated areas. On September 17, 2026, Regional Planning Director Amy Bodek ordered an immediate prohibition as interim guidance while the county writes it into the zoning code, following a motion by Board Chair Hilda Solis that supervisors approved unanimously in April. Solis says she will bring the zoning changes to the Board of Supervisors; no date has been set.

The push started in Monterey Park, where HMC StratCap proposed a data center of about 250,000 square feet at the vacant Saturn Business Park, 1977 Saturn Street. After packed meetings, the city adopted a 45-day moratorium in January, the developer withdrew in April, and on June 2 voters passed Measure NDC, which bans data centers unless future voters repeal it. "We had a victory landslide," said Steven Kung, co-founder of No Data Center Monterey Park. El Monte and Baldwin Park voted in April for yearlong bans.

Residents in Rowland Heights, Hacienda Heights, La Puente and other nearby communities are now fighting a possible data center at the mostly vacant Puente Hills Mall in the City of Industry, which has about 250 residents. In El Segundo, developer Eight Form withdrew a 50-megawatt plan to replace a Hyatt Place hotel at 750 N. Nash Street on July 9, after three hours of opposition at the planning commission.

Most of the county's data centers sit in El Segundo, downtown Los Angeles and Vernon, which runs its own power utility. In Vernon, Goodman Group has begun building LAX01, a 49.5-megawatt, three-level data center on 5.6 acres, and Digital Realty has bought land for a 32-megawatt building.

Clark County cannot legally ban or pause a data center, so what it does is attach conditions to new ones. In June 2026, commissioners approved Switch's LAS 19, a 56,800-square-foot building on nine acres near Warm Springs Road, next to the company's Core Campus, already the largest cluster of data center space in Southern Nevada. Switch agreed to help build a landscaped barrier separating a public sidewalk from Warm Springs Road traffic, after months of public comment.

Sierra Club biologist Marija Minic told commissioners data centers were "destroying communities, driving climate change, consuming resources and enriching tech billionaires"; Commissioner Michael Naft said the LAS 19 building would use closed-loop cooling with near-zero water use and run on renewable power. Commissioner Tick Segerblom pushed instead for a countywide ordinance on water and electricity use, and on July 7 commissioners said they would develop data center standards; the county has since tightened its heavy industrial zoning rules, the main tool it has.

The county's only other operating data center, Google's Henderson site, opened in 2020 and still uses evaporative cooling, which the Southern Nevada Water Authority banned for new commercial buildings in 2023. The Las Vegas Review-Journal called it the state's thirstiest data center, reporting 352 million gallons consumed in 2024; Google's own 2026 sustainability report puts the figure at 239.4 million gallons for 2025. Henderson's council rejected a proposed 180-day moratorium in July 2026 and told staff to add water, noise and setback rules to its development agreement process instead.

Gov. Joe Lombardo signed an executive order on September 19 requiring companies that want a state tax abatement to pay local school and sales taxes in full and meet local water standards. What happens next: Nevada legislators take up a statewide data center bill in 2027, and Clark County's new zoning standards are still being written.

Two large data center sites have come before local officials in Pinal County this year, with opposite results. On August 26, 2026 the Board of Supervisors voted 4-1 against rezoning land south of Eloy for Vermaland's La Osa Energy Center, which ended the project. In Casa Grande, the City Council voted 7-0 in early August to grant a waiver that lets a data center be built on about 480 acres north of Peters Road, between Bianco and Ethington roads, without the city's usual conditional use permit.

La Osa had already shrunk from 59 buildings to 11, served by a 500-megawatt gas plant and batteries, with a cap of 600 acre-feet a year on fresh water. So many people came to the hearing that the county opened five overflow rooms. "Many of my neighbors' wells have gone dry and require additional depth," said Mary Eileen Flanagan. Supervisor Stephen Miller argued that a no vote went against the Constitution and free-market principles. The county's zoning code still has no rules written for data centers, and residents are asking for them.

In Casa Grande, the council had required a conditional use permit for data centers in 2025. The owners of the Peters Road land, Vernon Barnes and Ethington & Hwy. 84 LLC, then filed claims under Arizona's Proposition 207 saying the change cut the value of their land. City Manager Larry Rains said the waiver protected taxpayers from a costly claim while keeping the permit rule for every other site.

The waiver caps drinking water for the data center and its on-site power plant at 800 acre-feet a year, against about 1,240 acre-feet the farmland uses now. It bans once-through cooling, requires yearly public water reports and limits generator testing to weekday daytime hours. Resident Casey Day, who lives across from the site, said the families nearby "have property rights too."

Union County has three Amazon Web Services data centers under construction in Jerome Township and Marysville, and a developer is now fighting to add two more nearby. Civil Solutions, a Cincinnati firm, filed in April for two campuses on about 215 acres in Jerome Township, on either side of the existing AWS site. The township's zoning inspector rejected both filings on September 3, and Civil Solutions has appealed to the Board of Zoning Appeals for December 17.

The existing AWS sites have taken a toll on emergency services: fire crews responded 84 times between 2021 and 2025, including two worker deaths and an April 2025 fire that burned for 30 hours and caused $50 million in damage, the Columbus Dispatch found. Crews were sometimes stopped by site security and made to wait outside for up to an hour; Amazon said it and its contractors added safety measures and blamed the delays on contractors' differing background-check rules.

Jerome Township trustees passed a moratorium on data center permits, but the zoning inspector kept approving them anyway, including two filed before the pause; residents packed a February 2026 meeting to object. On March 17 trustees voted to make data centers a conditional use, so each new application now has to be argued for individually.

In Marysville, the city council gave AWS a 30-year, 100 percent property tax exemption on March 10, 2025 for its two-building, 500,000-square-foot Project Cosmo campus, a $1 billion commitment. In exchange, AWS agreed to payments totaling about $15.6 million over 15 years, split between the city and the Marysville Exempted Village School District.

Plain City, which straddles the Union and Madison county line, adopted a six-month moratorium on new data center permits in August 2026, covering the village but not the unincorporated county around it. Union County Commissioner Tom McCarthy said in August that with opposition now close to universal, the balance may be shifting toward the communities.

Amazon and its builder, STACK Infrastructure, are putting two data center campuses in Caddo Parish, part of a Louisiana buildout that started with a $12 billion announcement in February 2026 for sites across Caddo and Bossier parishes and grew by $6 billion in August for a third campus, at the Resilient Technology Park by Interstate 20 in west Shreveport, bringing the state total to $18 billion. AWS has not disclosed that campus's power capacity or number of buildings. A legal challenge to the city's approval of the west Shreveport site is now before Louisiana's Second Circuit Court of Appeal, which is due to rule on November 18, 2026.

Most of Caddo Parish outside Shreveport and its five-mile planning boundary has no zoning at all, so a developer on unincorporated land needs no one's permission before building, which is why the parish commission's own attempts to slow things down have failed. Commissioner John-Paul Young's narrower resolution, asking the planning commission merely to consider recommending a moratorium, was voted down 6-4 on August 31, 2026; the commission has also declined to take up a one-year pause on developments drawing water from Caddo Lake.

The Shreveport campus went to court after the Metropolitan Planning Commission refused it a special use permit in December 2025 and the city council overturned that refusal. Mooringsport Mayor Tyler Gordon and two others sued, alleging the city withheld public information; a district judge dismissed their petition and upheld the permit in April 2026, and they appealed, backed by the Sierra Club.

Amazon says it will fund the water and wastewater upgrades its Louisiana projects need and has committed up to $400 million to public water systems in Caddo and Bossier parishes. Amazon director Keith Klein said in August, "Amazon pays its own way, and the communities where we operate will be better off because we're there." The Shreveport campus is expected to create about 210 permanent jobs and 2,250 construction jobs. Shreveport already has one small, unrelated data center operating, DartPoints, at about 2 megawatts.

The biggest data center planned in Polk County is Stonebridge's 4.4-million-square-foot campus on about 1,300 acres near U.S. Highway 17 and Broadway in Fort Meade, which would use more than 1,000 megawatts of power at full capacity. Fort Meade approved the rezoning and a tax break in 2025 and unanimously approved the development agreement in April 2026. It still needs a new water permit that the Southwest Florida Water Management District's board must approve at a public meeting.

Florida Commerce Secretary Alex Kelly wrote to Fort Meade that the plan is "fundamentally flawed" and its water use "woefully underestimated." Residents gathered more than 1,000 signatures to recall Mayor Jaret Williams, Vice Mayor Petrina McCutchen and Commissioner Mathew Taylor, and a residents' group has sued the city over its approval. The elections office certified the first round of recall signatures on August 14; Taylor sued on September 8 to stop the recall, and a judge had not ruled as of September 9.

In Lakeland, Project Swan, a proposed 600,000-square-foot data center on about 60 acres at 923 Wilkinson Road, is on hold under a one-year moratorium the City Commission passed 4-3 on August 3, 2026. The pause covers any business expected to use 50 megawatts or more, in the city and anywhere served by its utilities. For scale, Lakeland Electric's largest customer is a Publix complex using about 18 megawatts. All 16 residents who spoke backed a pause, and the three no votes wanted a narrower one. "Nothing wrong with pumping the brakes, guys," said Commissioner Guy LaLonde Jr.

In Haines City, Cielo Digital Infrastructure's plan for a 300-megawatt campus on about 74 acres at Marion Road and State Road 544 East is stalled because the fast-growing city has no spare water for the 150,000 gallons a day it would need. The city has received no formal application, and Deputy City Manager James Keene said the project is "still on step one."

Google is building a data center at 411 Pegasus Parkway in LaGrange, confirmed in April 2026 as the company's second in Georgia. Google says it will cover the full cost of the site's power and infrastructure and is funding utility upgrades for at least 50 LaGrange families. A second, unbuilt project, Fertile Ground Investments' proposed 600-megawatt campus near Hogansville, is still working through a land purchase and rezoning.

The Hogansville project, run by Fayetteville developer Luis Matta, would sit on 437 acres the city agreed to sell for $12,000 an acre under a non-disclosure agreement officials kept for 18 months; residents learned of it only after an open records request. "It's infuriating," said Hogansville resident Paula Darden. The city has since refused to rezone land for it: on August 17, 2026 the council voted 4-1 against creating a heavy industrial district, then extended its moratorium to a September 8 meeting; no outcome from that meeting has been published.

LaGrange rejected a separate $9.7 billion, 600-megawatt proposal called Project West in March 2025 when the council would not annex the 513 acres it needed. The city now requires a special-use permit for any new data center; one is pending for a 134-acre site on Pegasus Parkway proposed by the developer Fairpoint, recommended for approval by planners in July with a public hearing that was due by September 22.

Troup County itself adopted a 17-page ordinance in 2026 requiring a special-use permit for every data center, confining them to heavy industrial zoning with a 1,500-foot setback and Tier 4 diesel generators; the Troup County Anti-Data Center Coalition said it did not go far enough.

Kent County's most advanced data center proposal is Microsoft's, a planned $1 billion, 100-megawatt campus on 237 acres beside Interstate 96 in Lowell Charter Township, a community of about 6,500 people 20 miles southeast of Grand Rapids. A local business owner showed up to a December 2025 planning hearing in a Mr. Peanut costume holding a sign that said "This is nuts," and Microsoft introduced itself to the township in a January 7, 2026 letter, writing that "the community would like more information about the proposal." On May 18, 2026 the township board voted 2-5 against a moratorium on data centers and later formed a committee to draft its own ordinance.

West of Lowell, Microsoft also wants to rezone five parcels totaling about 104 acres off Patterson Avenue SE in Gaines Township, next to 320 acres it already owns there; this is the project listed in the table under Caledonia, its mailing address. Nearly 600 people packed a planning commission hearing at South Christian High School on April 15, 2026, and after hours of comment the commission tabled the rezoning; no decision has been made since. Microsoft's draft agreement offers a 65-decibel noise cap at property lines, a 150-foot building setback and a landscaped berm.

In the county's north end, Solon Township adopted a six-month moratorium on data centers in February 2026, and its planning commission has since tabled a proposed ordinance five times. "We want to reduce that down to 200 acres in the township," said Katie Valtchev of Stop Solon Township Data Center, of a draft that would allow 800 acres of data center development.

The county's other two tracked sites are Switch's Pyramid Campus in Grand Rapids, which is already operating, and Project Peninsula in Cedar Springs, a proposed site with no company or power figure reported yet. Gaines Township has not yet rescheduled a vote on the Microsoft rezoning, and Solon Township's planning commission is expected to take up its data center ordinance again next.
